better_edits.new: A list pattern `[p, q]` matches a `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `Array[T]` or `[T; N]` of exactly that many elements and binds each name to its element as above (`N` that can never equal the count is `E2020`, naming both); `[p, q, ..]` matches one with at least that many; `[p, ..rest]` names the remaining elements `rest`, a `Span[T]` of them (a `MutSpan[T]` where the scrutinee is a `ref mut` name of the list), a view like every pattern name, which the list's rules govern (`[BRW-1]`), and `[..rest]` alone names the whole; a `..rest` name reads its list in place, so under `match owns xs:` it is `E2020`, whose help is to match `xs` in place and take what is needed with `copy of rest` or `xs.drain(1..)`. A list pattern against a `String` or `StrView` is `E2020`, whose help gives `split`.
better_edits.why: The grammar produces list patterns and nothing says what they match or binds; the meaning follows the pattern default (names are views) and the one view type Ember has for a run of elements, and the two cases the reader's text left open (a fixed array of the wrong size, a `..rest` view of a list the match ends) are closed safely.

better_edits.old: | "[" [pattern {"," pattern}] ["," ".." [IDENT]] "]"
better_edits.new: | "[" [pattern {"," pattern}] ["," ".." [IDENT]] "]" | "[" ".." [IDENT] "]"   -- a list pattern ([GRM-13])
better_edits.why: `[..rest]` and `[..]` are the forms an empty-or-not test is written with, and the grammar cannot produce them; the reader's edit, kept.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed: the grammar produces `dyn Shape + Debug` and `some Iterator[Item = int] + Clone` ("`bound_list := type {"+" type} -- after `dyn` and `some` only`"), and no rule in the document says what such a value is: §IV.9 defines `dyn I` as "a data pointer and a table pointer" for one interface, DSP-3 "finds the interface's table through the type index" for one interface, TYP-32 defines `some I` for one, and no prose line writes `dyn A + B` anywhere (a search finds none). TYP-17 refuses `+` for bounds ("needs joined with `+`, is `E0100`") and says nothing of `dyn`, so an implementer cannot tell whether the grammar's `+` is meant or a leftover. The reader's edits are sound: the spelling follows verdict 109's sentence "The same spelling goes everywhere a list of needs is written", though that verdict's own scope is `needs` lists (109 to 112), so extending it to `dyn`/`some` is the lead's ruling under the delegation (AUTOPILOT §3: "Record an owner's answer in exactly the owner's scope, never wider"), to be marked as such or put to the owner beside `[T: needs (Add, Copy)]`; `dyn (A, B)` has the same shape as `needs (A, B)` against a tuple type, which `needs` already resolves by meaning. The layout keeps `dyn` at two words and DSP-3's call, so no §X.4 row changes. Two things the reader's TYP-22 text leaves for an implementer to guess are added below: which package writes the set's table (BLD-16: "No fact of the whole program decides a package's code or layout"; the package that converts at TYP-5 rule 8's site knows both the type and the set, and MNG-4's naming lets the linker keep one), and whether a `dyn (A, B)` value goes to a `dyn A` place (TYP-5 rule 8 reads "a value to an interface its type implements", which through `dyn` is unknown, so without a word it is `E2020`).

better_edits.old: bound_list    := type {"+" type}                        -- after `dyn` and `some` only
better_edits.new: bound_list    := type | "(" type {"," type} [","] ")"     -- after `dyn` and `some`: one bare, several in round brackets, as `needs` ([TYP-17], [TYP-22])
better_edits.why: The reader's edit, kept: one spelling for a list of interfaces, resolved against a tuple type by meaning as `needs` is.

better_edits.old:
A bound without `needs`, or needs joined with `+`, is `E0100`, whose
  message gives the line with `needs` (`[T: Add + Copy]` gives `[T: needs (Add, Copy)]`).
better_edits.new: A bound without `needs`, or needs joined with `+`, is `E0100`, whose message gives the line with `needs` (`[T: Add + Copy]` gives `[T: needs (Add, Copy)]`); interfaces joined with `+` after `dyn` or `some` are `E0100` too, whose message gives the brackets (`owns dyn Shape + Debug` gives `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`; after `dyn` and `some` the brackets stand without `needs`, the word before them saying what the value is).
better_edits.why: The reader's edit, kept: the refusal and its line to write go where the rule for the spelling is.

better_edits.new: `dyn (A, B)` is a value of one type implementing every listed interface, each of which is itself usable as `dyn`, held with one data pointer and one table pointer as `dyn I` is. The table of the set for a type is written by the package that converts a value of that type to `dyn (A, B)` (`[TYP-5]` rule 8), which sees both, under one symbol per set and type (`[MNG-4]`), so the linker keeps one copy (`[MONO-1]`) and every package lays it out and reads it alike (`[BLD-16]`): first the type's index (`[TYP-44a]`), then a pointer to each listed interface's own table for the type, then `A`'s entries and `B`'s, each interface's in its declaration order. A call through it is `[DSP-3]`'s, one indirect call; a kind test is one compare, as on `dyn I`; a `dyn (A, B)` value given to a `dyn A` place converts by `[TYP-5]` rule 8 with one load of the member's table pointer, and to a `dyn C` of an interface not listed it is `E2020`. `some (A, B)` is one concrete type meeting both, with no table (`[TYP-32]`). One interface takes no brackets (`owns dyn Shape`).
better_edits.why: The reader's layout, with the two facts an implementer still had to guess: who writes the table (so that `[BLD-16]` holds) and what a value of several interfaces converts to; the member-table pointers make the conversion one load at the cost of a few words per table, nothing per call.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed: TYP-47 "`Cs...` among type arguments spells the pack's types out (`View[Cs...]`)" and the grammar (`generic_arg := ... | IDENT "..."`; `tuple_type := "(" ")" | "(" type "," type {"," type} [","] ")"`; `fn_type_param := [param_word] type`) let a pack be spelled out only as a type argument, so the item type of the library's own `View[Cs...]` (ECS-4: "gives each item read-only (`for e, a, b in reg.view[A, B]():`)", a type written nowhere) and verdict 115's named uses ("a tuple's interfaces written once for every size (Rust stops at 12), events and callbacks passing several values (`Event[int, String]` with handlers `fn(int, String)`)") cannot be written; TYP-27 "a tuple type has two or more elements (ODR-071)" leaves `View[Position]`'s and `zip(xs)`'s item (STD-26: "`zip(a, b, …)` (any number of iterables ...)") undecided for one and none; a search for `(Entity, `, `Ts...)` or `Item = (` in the document finds nothing. The reader's edits are at the cause, add no spelling beyond C++'s (verdict 116: "A pack is written with C++'s dots"), keep TYP-27 (no one-element tuple, as the E0100 row says of `(e,)`), and run nothing (TYP-47: "Each use is made for its exact types ... nothing is looked up while the program runs"). Verdict 115's "no tuple" speaks of the brackets (`view[Position]`, not `view[(Position,)]`), so the one-and-none sizes are the lead's to rule, as the reader says; option B would contradict TYP-27 and the E0100 row.

Decided by composition, as the reader says: LEX-14 "A raw identifier `r#name` uses a keyword as a name (for imported C fields such as `type`)"; LEX-15 "**Reserved and not words of Ember** (lexed as keywords so that no program uses them as names; any use is `E1010`, whose message gives the word to write): `owned` ... and `self`" and "**Reserved for a future version** (lexed as keywords; using one as a name is `E0005` ...): `async`, `await`, `macro`"; the FFI table (§XVI.3) "| an identifier that is an Ember keyword | a raw identifier `r#type` (`[LEX-14]`) |". The reserved words are lexed as keywords, a keyword is what `r#` turns into a name, and the importer maps every keyword identifier to `r#`, so a C field `owned` is reachable only as `b.r#owned`; the other reading (that `r#owned` is a "use" of the word) would make an imported field unreachable, which the FFI table's row rules out. Not a defect; the reader's four-word clarification would be harmless.

LEX-18, changed in 0.9.20, decides it in words: "After `.` the lexer reads an integer, never a float: `t.0.1` is two field accesses", and the grammar's `postfix := ... | "." IDENT | "." INT`. So `edges[0].0.1` is `(edges[0].0).1`. Nothing remains.

missed.title: A whole name as an element of a collection literal: handed over, viewed or refused?
missed.rules: TYP-38, EXP-6, OWN-9. EXP-6 lists the uses that hand a whole name over: "used as a value (given with `=`, given to an `owns` parameter, returned, captured with `owns`)"; OWN-9 adds "`return a` hands `a` over with no word, and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does: `w = Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over"; TYP-38 says only "Every element converts to the element type by `[TYP-5]`" and "An element for a list of `owns` values is made with `owns`". A collection literal's element is in none of these lists, so for `xs = [a, b]` with `a: String` an implementer cannot say whether `a` ends (`E3040` after), whether `xs` is an `Array[ref String]` of views (which TYP-15 would allow a list to hold), or whether the line is refused.

    b = String("bob")
    xs = [a, b]          # hands `a` and `b` over, or an Array[ref String] of views?
    println(a)           # E3040, or prints "ann"?
    xs.push(owns String("cy"))

`w =
  Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over, `Point(x=a)` copies `a`.
edits.new: `w = Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over, `Point(x=a)` copies `a`; an element of a collection literal is given the same way (`xs = [a, b]` hands `a` and `b` over and a later use of `a` is `E3040`; `[copy of a, b]` keeps `a`; a `Copy` value is copied; a part, or a value reached through a name that does not own it, is `E3013` as elsewhere, `[OWN-11]`).

missed.title: `owns dyn I`: which of a required interface's implementations it has
missed.rules: TYP-36, TYP-22. TYP-36's prose gives `owns dyn I` exactly two things, "`owns dyn I` when `I` requires `Clone`" and "`owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq`", and the table has no row for it, so `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` are read from an omission; but TYP-22 reaches "a method of an interface that `I` requires ... through `dyn I` ... where it names `Self` nowhere but as `this`" and allows one `dyn` entry for a method "generic over a type parameter used only as the type of a parameter that views its value (a plain or `ref mut` parameter)", which `Display.fmt`, `Debug.fmt` and `Hash.hash[H: needs Hasher](ref mut h: H)` are, so by TYP-22 `owns dyn I` would have `Display`, `Debug` and `Hash` where `I` requires them, and by TYP-36's silence it would not. An implementer choosing `E2040` or acceptance for `Set[owns dyn Shape]` or `println(shape)` with `interface Shape: needs (Debug, Hash):` cannot tell which rule governs.
missed.program:
interface Shape: needs (Debug, Hash, Ord):
    fn area() -> float

fn main():
    seen: Set[owns dyn Shape] = Set()      # needs Eq and Hash on `owns dyn Shape`: TYP-22 reaches `hash`, TYP-36 grants only Clone and Eq
    shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape] = []
    shapes.sort()                          # needs Ord: `cmp(other: Self)` is E2050 through dyn, so E2040 here, by inference only
    println(shapes)                        # Debug through dyn: TYP-22 yes, TYP-36 silent

edits.old:
`owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq`
  (`interface Shape: needs Eq:`, a method-table entry as for `Clone`): values of two different kinds
  are never equal, and two of one kind compare their contents; that entry is the one way `Eq` is
  reached through `dyn` (`[TYP-22]`).
edits.new: `owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq` (`interface Shape: needs Eq:`, a method-table entry as for `Clone`): values of two different kinds are never equal, and two of one kind compare their contents; that entry is the one way `Eq` is reached through `dyn` (`[TYP-22]`). Of the other interfaces `I` requires, `owns dyn I` (and `shares dyn I`, `shares mut dyn I`, `dyn I` where a view may stand) has those whose methods `[TYP-22]` reaches through `dyn`, `Display`, `Debug` and `Hash` (each method names `Self` only as `this`, and `hash`'s hasher is a parameter that views its value, so it gets one entry), and never `Ord` (`cmp` takes `other: Self`): a bound needing `Ord` on it is `E2040`, whose help is `sort_by` with the kinds tested first.
edits.why: Two rules answer the question in different ways by silence; one sentence makes TYP-36 say what TYP-22's mechanism gives, so the `—` of a missing row is no longer the only evidence.

missed.title: A pack spelled out inside a type built on each member (`Option[Cs]...`) is not producible
missed.rules: TYP-47, grammar generic_arg. Verdict 116 chose "C++'s spelling", and TYP-47 says "`Cs...` among type arguments spells the pack's types out (`View[Cs...]`)"; the grammar's `generic_arg := ... | IDENT "..."` spells out only a bare pack name, so a type formed over each member, C++'s pattern expansion (`Option[Cs]...`, `Span[Cs]...`), is not producible, and the text does not say whether that is meant. The ECS's own `View` would want it for a method giving each component as an `Option` (`try_get -> (Option[Cs]...)`) and a library `zip` of spans (`Span[Ts]...`) cannot be typed. Not a safety matter; an implementer cannot tell whether a refusal is the design or a gap.
missed.program:
[Cs...]
struct View:
    reg: ref Registry
    fn try_get(e: Entity) -> (Option[Cs]...):     # `Option[Cs]...` is no generic_arg, tuple element or pattern the grammar has
        pass

edits.new: `...` is written after a pack's name only (`Cs...`, `values...`); a type formed over each type of the pack (`Option[Cs]...`, C++'s pattern expansion) is not Ember, and is `E0100`, whose help is a second pack or a tuple of the spelled-out pack (`(Option[Cs]...)` is not it either; write the type the use needs, `[Os...]` above the function, with `Os` the options).
edits.why: The grammar refuses it today; saying so, with its reason, keeps an implementer from reading the owner's "C++'s spelling" as C++'s whole pack grammar. The lead may instead rule the expansion in; then `generic_arg`, `tuple_elem` and `fn_type_param` take `type "..."` where the type names exactly one pack, and TYP-47 says it is written out once per member, nothing running for it (`[MONO-1]`).

answered_by.quote: A call says `ref mut` before an argument the callee may change, and `owns` before one it takes over, with the same words as the parameter, `const` included: ... `take(owns xs)` for `fn take(owns xs: Array[int]):`, whatever is given

A function from a variable given to a parameter whose type is a type parameter bounded by a function type (`owns f: F` under `[F: needs fn(int)]`, `[CLO-14]`), in any package, is lent for the call: `F` names that very function, the callee runs it and keeps nothing of it, so after `xs.iter().for_each(h)` and after `apply(h)` alike `h` is the caller's still.

a value the call gives back that keeps the lent function (an iterator adapter, `[STD-19]`) is a value holding a view of `h`, which lives no longer than `h` (`[LT-45]`). A parameter of a callable type (`owns f: fn(int)`) keeps what it is given and takes `owns` as any `owns` parameter does.

`thread.spawn` runs a function on a new thread, which may outlive the function that started it. It takes a function any thread may run, `[R]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`

Standard-library functions that keep a function beyond the call, or run it on another thread, take it `owns`: `thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R` (`[THR-10]`, `[JOB-2]`), a callback registry an `owns` function value

A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word, as to any function that takes it as a type parameter (`[FN-2a]`): after `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is the caller's still and `h(5)` runs it (ODR-240).

before an argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given (`take(owns xs)`, `take(owns copy of xs)`, `take(owns [1, 2])`, `xs.iter().for_each(owns fn(x: int): println(x))`; `[FN-2a]`, `E3028` without it)
`names.push(owns p.name)` a part (`[OWN-11]`)
A named function, or a lambda that captures nothing, has no state and allocates nothing, and is `Copy`; a function value with state is not, and `=` hands it over.

A value `=` copies (a number, a `bool`, a `char`, a `StrView`, a `ref T`, a `Span[T]`, a struct made only of these) is copied with `=` too, so `b = owns n` is how `=` hands one over: `n` ends there, and a later use is `E3040`
It is a value of its function type and may be passed by its name, so a long lambda may be written inside the call or as a local function passed by its name (`a = thread.spawn(push_a)`).
or as a local function (`fn push_a() thread_shared log:` with the body `log.push("a")`, then `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`).

clusters.program: J3-02's program as the rules now read: `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` is `E3028` (`spawn`'s parameter is `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R`, a callable type, not an `F`-bounded one, so `[FN-2a]`'s loan does not apply); `a = thread.spawn(owns push_a)` compiles, hands the local function over, and `push_a()` after it is `E3040`. J6-12's program: `b.handlers.push(beep)` and `b.on_click(beep)` are both `E3028` (`push(owns value: T)` by verdict 149 and `[FN-2a]`'s `names.push(owns p.name)`; `on_click(owns f: Handler)` is "a parameter of a callable type ... takes `owns`"); `b.handlers.push(owns beep)` ends `beep` (it captures nothing, so it is `Copy`, and `owns` is how a copied value is handed over), `b.handlers.push(owns copy of beep)` keeps it. `return xs.iter().map(h)` is a value holding a view of `h` (`[LT-45]`, `E3063` where it would outlive `h`). The only thing left is that `[CLO-12]` and `[GRM-28]` still print `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`, the refused spelling, as working code.

edits.new: with the body `log.push("a")`, then `a = thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, with the call's word as for every argument for an `owns` parameter, since `spawn` keeps the function past the call (`[THR-10]`, `[FN-2a]`); after it `push_a` is handed over and `push_a()` is `E3040`; `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` is `E3028`, "`spawn` takes `push_a` over (its first line says `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R`); say so at the call: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`").

edits.new: a local function passed by its name (`a = thread.spawn(owns push_a)`; the call says the parameter's word, `[FN-2a]`, and a local function given to an `F`-bounded parameter is lent with no word, `for_each(push_a)`).

clusters.departs_from_verdict: None in substance; two verdicts' own words are narrowed, and the text already did so in Hardened_2 (H.53: "a function from a variable given to an `F`-bounded parameter is lent in any package"). Verdict 51's example line reads `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` with no word; verdict 147 (later, "whatever is passed") adds `owns` at the call, so the local-function form 51 allows is kept and spelled `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`. Verdict 150's general words ("a standard-library function is borrowed") are narrowed to a parameter the library runs during the call (`F`-bounded): `thread.spawn` cannot borrow a function it may outlive (`[THR-10]`), and verdict 149 makes `push` take `owns`; 150's own example (`for_each(h)`) stands.

answered_by.quote: `return a` and a constructor's argument take no word: they hand a value over as `=` does (`[OWN-9]`).
`return a` hands `a` over with no word, and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does: `w = Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over, `Point(x=a)` copies `a`.
`fn init(…)` is the constructor; it sets the fields of the object it builds through `this`, with no word.
`fn init(…)` on a struct is its constructor; it sets the fields through `this`, with no word.

`owns` is not written before a name whose place already hands the value over, after `return`, nor before `fn` written on its own, nor before a value made on the line for a place that is not an `owns T` (`[GRM-15]`) (`E0109`: "`e.mesh = m` already hands `m` over; remove `owns`"
`Emitter("fountain")` passes a string literal where a `String` is expected; the literal allocates the `String` there (`[TXT-9]`), and `owns name` takes it over.
A missing word, or one written where the parameter does not say it, is `E3028` ("`bump` may change `a` (its first line says `ref mut c: Counter`); say so at the call: `bump(ref mut a)`"
A parameter with no word reads.
A hand-over out of a name or place that does not own the value is `E3013` too: "`v.push(owns template)` would hand over the caller's player, but `template` only reads it

clusters.program:
The `owns` half is decided: a written `init` is "the constructor" (`[CLS-2]`, `[STR-6]`), so `Emitter(label)` for `fn init(owns name: String):` compiles and hands `label` over, `Emitter(owns label)` is `E0109`, as verdict 159 says and I.5 shows. Two implementer questions remain, both from the same sentence of `[FN-2a]`.

Both sentences apply to this line and give different verdicts.
(2) `class Widget:` with `fn init(ref mut registry: Registry): registry.add(weakref this)` — hmm, `this` as a whole before every field is set is `E2100`, so take `fn init(ref mut registry: Registry, owns name: String): this.name = name` then `registry.count += 1`; in `main`: `w = Widget(ref mut reg, label)` or `w = Widget(reg, label)`. `[FN-2a]`'s first sentence makes the missing `ref mut` `E3028`; its "a constructor's argument take[s] no word" exempts a constructor's argument from any word. Which is written cannot be decided from the text, and verdict 1 ("A call that changes an argument says so") needs the word.

The edit keeps verdict 159 where it was decided (no `owns`, hand over) and lets the `init`'s first line say what happens otherwise, which is the owner's rule for every other call (verdicts 1, 3, 147).

and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does: `w =
  Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over, `Point(x=a)` copies `a`.

The hole is real. `[CLO-10]`: "A function value is two words, `{code, state}`. Its state is what it needs besides its code: what it captured with a word, in one block of its own ... except that a state of one word or less that the function's body never writes is kept in the state word itself ... and where the real variables it uses live, which costs nothing beyond their addresses." For `pull`, which uses the real `gravity` and `dt`, "where the real variables it uses live" is two addresses in a one-word state; "costs nothing" forbids a block, yet nothing names the one-word shape that makes two addresses cost nothing, and for `drag` (a one-word `copy of k` plus the real `dt`) the state word is already taken, so a block or not is left to the implementer, and with it `E4001` in `@noalloc fall` ("`Alloc` is at the line that makes the function value ... and `E4001` there names it"), which `[PHIL-13]` forbids to vary. The reader's shape (the maker's frame address in the state word; a block only where a word-capture and real variables meet) is the cheapest general one and keeps `[CLO-4]` (the value ends before the frame). Narrowed on wording and on one consequence. (1) "since every real variable it uses belongs to that function" is false for a lambda inside a local function that uses the outer function's variable (`[CLO-2]` lets a local function use its maker's variables and a lambda in it use them again): the one address still suffices, reached through the local function's own frame and state word, so the sentence should say the real variables are reached through that frame, not that they belong to it. (2) The message's "give `k` to it as a parameter" would change the callable type `fn(ref mut Particle)` the place has; "use the real `k`" is the help. (3) The X.4 row must also say what the rule costs a program the spec itself writes: `scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: total += t.split_whitespace().count())` (`[THR-17]`) captures `ref t` and uses the real `total`, so under this rule each task's function has a block; that is inherent in a two-word function value (today `fn() copy of a, copy of b` has one too) and belongs in the row, not hidden. A `thread_shared` value's block always comes from the runtime allocator (`[RT-1]`), whatever manager its class names: `thread_shared` before a value made `using m` is `E2114` ("a `thread_shared` value's block carries its making thread's record, which only the runtime allocator keeps; remove `using m`: `names = thread_shared Names()`").
A `thread_shared` value is never placed in a frame, and never in a memory manager's instance: its making thread is read from its chunk (`[RC-4]`), which only the runtime allocator's blocks have.

A `thread_shared` value made `using` an instance (`[ALC-1]`) lies in memory the runtime did not lay out, so it is marked handed over at the line that makes it (`[RC-4]` point 4) and no thread asks which thread made it.

A `thread_shared` value made `using` an instance of a manager that may have several instances (`[ALC-1]`) is marked handed over at the line that makes it: its instance may be reset or end as soon as the compiler sees its last owner end (`[ALC-5]`, `[LT-4]`), which an end delayed to a check point would miss, so every owner of such a value is counted in its away count and its end is never delayed; a value made in `Global` or `System` keeps the two counts, its block waits for the check point and nothing reuses it.

    safe fn create_window() -> *mut u8

The grammar accepts both (`fn_header := ["extern" STRING] ["unsafe"] ["static" | "virtual" | "override"] ["gen"]`). [UNS-12] makes the body unsafe code ("Its body is unsafe code, as the inside of an `unsafe:` block is"), and [UNS-11] says who must vouch: "before a declaration (`unsafe fn`, ...) it says that whoever uses it must vouch, with `@safety` saying what they must make true". The user of a `drop` is the value's end, which [DRP-1] places ("runs exactly once per value, at the end of its life") and no line names; [UNS-1]'s `E3100` is for "call an `unsafe fn`" outside unsafe code, and no rule says whether the end of `w` in safe code is such a call. [CLS-7a]'s "A `drop`'s first line is `fn drop():`" gives no code for `unsafe fn drop():`. For the override, [CLS-4] checks only `virtual`/`override` (`E2110`, `E2111`) and [DSP-2] sends the safe call `ws[0].show()` to the unsafe body with no one vouching. So the text accepts a program in which `@safety`'s obligation is made true by nobody, which is what [UNS-11]'s "possible only inside an `unsafe` block" promises against. The reader's edit is at the cause (where the mismatch is declared), refuses only the three forms safe code reaches without naming them, keeps an `unsafe` virtual or interface method callable as any `unsafe fn` is, and adds no code; `E2020` is [FN-6]'s "an `unsafe fn` where a safe one is wanted", a fair fit, and which code is the lead's (JOB.md: messages and codes are the lead's). No verdict is touched: 118 and 119 say what an `unsafe fn` is, not where one may be declared. It also covers `Display.fmt` run by `println` and `Add.add` run by `+`, which are implementations of interface methods declared without `unsafe`.

The text decides both programs as the lead ruled (decisions.md §4, area 2 Q4: "across a call, only 'not ended or moved' is checked (BRW-21); a change through a link is allowed, and the compiler never assumes the value unchanged (verdict 18, the turret)"). J5-07: [WK-11] "any name may make one (`up = weakref p` from a read-only `p` ...)", [GRM-44] "`if ui exists as ref mut me:` may change what it names"; inside `inspect`, `e` is not used after `w = weakref e` (a link is not a view, so [BRW-2]'s liveness does not extend `e`), and [BCK-3]'s "when they lead to values of one type and at least one path goes through a link" would give `E3021` only while `e` is live; the caller holds no view of `boss`. So it compiles and prints 0. J4-14: [BRW-21] "Writing a number or a `bool` ends and moves nothing" and "Since a `ref mut` parameter is compiled with noalias (`[BRW-22]`), the check is wider for it", so for a plain `p` the call check is end-or-move only, and [BRW-17] defers the parameter/module-variable case to the call ("A view parameter (a plain, `Span` or `ref mut` one), or `this`, and what its function may end or move may be one place too; that is checked at each call"); prints 5. The promise [FN-1] states, "what `a` reads does not change while `a` is used (`[BRW-1]`)", is therefore wider than what is checked, and the reader's two edits write the ruling where the promise is made. Safe: a scalar written through another name dangles nothing, every view the caller holds is checked by the type rule of [BCK-3] and [BRW-17] against the callee's summary, and a plain parameter has no noalias. The edits narrow verdict 5 ("A read-only name is a promise that what it reads does not change while it is in use") across a call only, which is the lead's standing ruling, so no owner verdict is overridden; the lead should still mark it in the change log as the ruling's consequence.

[EXP-4] names the lives of temporaries of "an expression statement", of "the **condition** of an `if`, `elif` or `while`", of `with` and of a `for` iterable, and never a `match` subject; the grammar makes `match_stmt` a `compound_stmt`, not an expression statement, so [DRP-3] decides ("Temporaries drop at the end of the statement that created them"): the guard lives through `job.run()`. [THR-19] then refuses only while "this thread holds a lock, inside its `with` block, or from `g = m.lock()`, `g = rw.read()` or `g = rw.write()` to the last use of `g` or of a value holding it", and the E7018 row repeats the two forms ("its `with` block, or a guard in a local until its last use"); a guard that is a temporary is neither, so `job.run()`, "a direct call that may take the held lock and is not proved to enter past it", is not refused and the program waits for ever, against the rule's title "A wait for a lock this thread holds is refused when compiling" (verdict 43). Deadlock is permitted by [PHIL-11] in general, but this one is the kind verdict 43 promises to refuse, so the text is not answered. The reader's edits are safe and at the cause: [THR-19] gains the missing holding form (the compiler already tracks a temporary's life, [BRW-19]), and [EXP-4] gives the `match` subject the condition rule, under which `match owns JOBS.lock().pop():` lets the guard go before the arm (the arm's name owns the popped value and views nothing of the guard) while `match JOBS.lock().first():` keeps it to the end of the arm whose name views it. Nothing runs. Note for the lead: whether `owns` before a temporary subject is `E0109` is K22's question; the [EXP-4] edit holds either way.

The rules pull apart. The caller's name ends" and [RC-1] speaks of "an `owns` parameter, which this function owns from its first line". It is the only answer [BLD-16] allows ("No fact of the whole program decides a package's code or layout"): a link to an implementer declared in another package cannot make that package lay out a weak count. Safe and free. The [DSP-4] edit only aligns its list with [TYP-44]'s ("`dyn I`, `owns dyn I`, `shares dyn I`, `shares mut dyn I`"). `sharedref mut dyn I` is a separate small gap, listed under missed.

[SPN-5] promises "on a `MutSpan` it lends the view and returns two disjoint `MutSpan`s"; [SPN-3] requires "A name or parameter that writes a `MutSpan`'s elements says `ref mut` (`d = ref mut a.as_mut_span()` ...), and a plain one only reads them (`E3023`, `[BRW-15]`)"; [BRW-12] lets `ref mut` stand "before a `MutSpan` a call gives", one span; [GRM-5]'s targets are bare (`target := IDENT | postfix_expr | "_" | "(" target_list ")"`), so `ref mut left, ref mut right = ...` does not parse and `left, right = ref mut samples.split_at(mid)` is `ref mut` before a tuple that no rule names. The one-branch `match` with `(ref mut left, ref mut right)` is plausible under [GRM-13] but the text does not say a `ref mut` pattern name on a temporary's `MutSpan` part writes its elements, and it is not the line `E3023`'s help would give. So an implementer cannot write both halves and the question stands. The reader's edit is safe (the halves are disjoint by [SPN-5] and [BRW-4], both names may be live together, checked when compiling), costs nothing, keeps the word on the value as verdict 34's own example does (`d = ref mut tracks[dst_name].as_mut_span()`), and adds no second place for words on an `=` line.

Using the parent while a scope is live is `E3096`, whose help is to allocate from the scope"; `[LT-46]`: "`ref mut T` may change, and it is alone: while its holder is still used, the place is not read or changed through any other name". Both halves are decided as the reader says, and the current shape is forced, not a free design choice. `[HR-16]`: "`old` is a read-only view of the old instance"; `[OWN-11]`: "A hand-over out of a name or place that does not own the value is `E3013` too", so `sock=old.sock` and `sock=owns old.sock` (which by verdict 159 "works as `=` does" for a non-`Copy` value) are `E3013`, while `target=shares old.target` is admitted (`[HR-16]`: "A `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` link read from `old` may be stored into the new instance's field ... it names the old instance until commit, and commit's map (`[HR-2a]`) repoints it"). verdicts.reason: Both programs are accepted and break promises. The reader is right that the memory-safety routes are closed today (`[THR-1]` `E7014` for a direct push into a `thread_shared` object, `[THR-20]` `E7012` for an unguarded `static mut` a `drop` a function on another thread may run changes), so the hole is the promise of `[THR-19]`. (2) `[RC-4]` point 3 places check points only in compiled code and "when the thread ends"; a job worker waiting for work and a host thread back in C (`[FFI-22]`, `[HR-3a]`) reach none, and `[THR-16]` runs no `drop` at the process's end, so the `Asset`'s `close` never runs, against `[OWN-2]` "A value always ends with its clean-up" and point 5's own promise. Confirmed as not answered. The reader's fix is narrowed because its placement rule is lexical ("outside every `with` block of a lock, and after a guard's last use") while the property it claims ("where this thread holds no lock") is not: a function with a loop called from inside `with pool.lock:` has a back edge the compiler places a check point at, since the callee cannot see its caller's lock (`[BLD-16]`: no fact outside the package's own text decides its code), and the queued `Conn`'s `drop` waits there for the lock this thread holds; the same for a blocking call in such a callee. So the proposed text reopens J7-01 one call down, or forces an implementer to add a thread-local lock-depth test the cost table has no row for. The better fix moves the decision to the type, where the declaring package can see it and `[BLD-16]` allows it: a `thread_shared` value whose `drop` (or the `drop` of anything it owns) may take a lock, join a thread or end a scope, the things `[THR-19]` refuses under a held lock, is marked handed over at its making line, as a value made `using` an instance already is (`[RC-4]` point 4, N84), so every owner of it is counted atomically and "**A `drop` runs where the last owner ends**" (`[THR-20]`) is literally true for it: the `drop` runs on the thread that ends the last owner, where `[THR-19]`, `[THR-11]` and `[DRP-8]` judge it as the call it is, and the queue holds only values whose `drop` waits for nothing, so a check point anywhere, under a lock or in a callee, waits for nothing. This refuses no program, adds nothing checked while running, keeps biased counting for every type whose `drop` only frees, closes files or touches atomics, and costs atomic counts for the lock-taking types alone (a row below). It also removes the contradiction that sank the earlier design (its arbiter's E3-1, a scoped task's last pending destructors against the scope's end): nothing lock-taking is ever deferred to a scope's end. The reader's two J7-02 provisions are kept (a worker empties its queue before each wait for work and is woken by a value put in it; a value made on a host thread is marked handed over, which the runtime does when it gives out the block, since it knows the thread from its registration and the compiler emits nothing new), as is "for `main`, before its return ends the process". A `thread.spawn` thread blocked for a long time in a receive or a join delays the lock-free values queued to it (new-gaps NG-11, NG-47); that is the delay verdict 101 itself states ("at its next check point") and `[PHIL-11]`'s resource matter, never a lost clean-up, so no edit.

The reader's fix keeps verdict 105 (the task's own total, in the place's type, stops on overflow) and verdict 77's example. Narrowed for three things: (1) "`+=` and `-=` counting as one" does not work with "the accumulator gathers what the task takes away" on an unsigned place (`P -= 3; P += 5` on a `u8` would gather `0 - 3` and stop where one by one gives 12), so the two must count as one operator only on a signed place, where the accumulator holds the signed change from 0; (2) for `max`, `min`, `&` and `|` a flag for "gave none" is not needed: these are idempotent, so the accumulator starts from the place's value at the spawn, which nothing changes before the join (`[THR-21]` "Nothing reads the place before the join", `[THR-11]`), and a task whose statement never runs leaves the place as it is; this also settles a float `max` with a `NaN` without a `-inf` start and keeps `[DET-2]`; (3) the Map sentence "inserting a key absent from `P` with the accumulator's value" gives the wrong sign once `-=` gathers what is taken away, and must say what applying the accumulator to the type's zero gives. fn crc_of(i: u32) -> u32:
    c = i
    for _ in 0..8:
        c = (c >> 1) ^ (0xEDB88320 & (0 - (c & 1)))
    return c

fn crc_table() -> [u32; 256]:
    t: [u32; 256] = [0; 256]
    unsafe:
        p = t.as_mut_ptr()                 # a pointer into the evaluator's heap, never leaving it
        for i in 0..256:
            p.add(i).write(crc_of(i as u32))
    return t

const CRC: [u32; 256] = comptime(crc_table())

comptime:                                  # the same writes, written in the block itself
    u: [u32; 4] = [0; 4]
    unsafe:
        u.as_mut_ptr().write(7)
    assert(u[0] == 7)

better_edits.new:
Each use of a C++ name of several functions (as `[FFI-30]` counts them) stands for the one it
  fits exactly: a call (`new`, `super.init(…)`, a method, a function of a namespace) by its
  arguments' number, names, types and words, an untyped literal counting as the type C++ gives it
  (`c_int`, `f64`); an `override fn` by its parameters' types; a function value by its expected
  callable type; an overlay entry by what it writes (`[GRM-35]`). No conversion but a literal's
  typing takes part, so a use fits one function or none, as C++ would pick it or refuse. Two methods
  alike but for the method's own `const` are one Ember method, as `operator[]`'s pair is `Index` and
  `IndexMut` (`[FFI-42]`): a call runs the `const` one, and the other where the call's result is
  assigned through, given `ref mut`, or has a method called on it that changes its object
  (`[FFI-40]`), so the choice is read from the use and never from what the object's name permits
  (such a use through a name that only reads the object is `E3023`); one overlay entry covers the
  pair, its `@ffi(const)` speaking of the `const` one (`[FFI-40a]`). What the code around the use
  permits (`unsafe`, effects, hand-overs, threads, views) is checked after, on the one chosen, so a
  line runs the same function wherever it stands. A use that none fits, or that two fit, is `E5070`,
  naming each C++ declaration ("`r.draw(x)`: `Renderer::draw(const Mesh&)` and
  `Renderer::draw(const Sprite&)` both take `x` as written; give `x` the type of one"); an entry so
  placed is `E5010`. `super.init(…)` runs the constructor it selects at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`);

better_edits.why: The reader's rule with the `const` pair decided by the result's use (the nearest rule, `[FFI-42]`), which removes the circularity through `this` and lets one entry vouch for the pair; exact fits only, so C++'s widening never changes which function an override or call means.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed as an implementer question. `[FN-2a]`: "A parameter of a callable type (`owns f: fn(int)`) keeps what it is given and takes `owns` as any `owns` parameter does", and "a function written in the call is given with `owns` (verdict 158)"; `[FFI-21]` under `callback(retained)`: "the function value, its code and its state, is moved into a block of its own" — a hand-over — yet the parameter in `[FFI-52]`'s example is plain, `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)`, and the call `register_cb(fn() owns game: game.add_point())` writes no word. For `register_cb(add)` with a named `add` holding `owns game`, nothing says whether `add` ends (`E3040` at the next use) or is usable, and an implementer who lets it be used reads a moved value. The reader's `[FFI-21]` edit (an `owns` parameter under `retained`/`once`, `owns` at the call, `E3028` without it) is at the cause and follows verdicts 147 and 158. Its `[FFI-10]` edit, though, makes the C pointer type the written type of a `callback(…)` parameter ("written as the C function pointer it is ... `owns cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void)`"), an exception to the rule's own sentence that a `safe fn` "writes the safe Ember types and the words in front of its parameters' names (`ref mut`, `owns`) produced by those words; the compiler checks that mapping and lowers it to the C ABI carrier", while `[FFI-21]` already names the safe type ("The callable type of a `callback(…)` parameter is `fn(P…) -> R`"). A `Span[T]` parameter is written as `Span[T]` with its witness `n` in C form (ODR-074); the callback is the same shape: the callable type written, the user-data witness in C form. So the better fix writes `owns cb: fn()` (the finder's A) and keeps the reader's `[FFI-21]` and message edits. No cost while running.

verdicts.reason: The two lines are undecided as the reader says. `[FFI-8]`: "A `handle` is an opaque pointer-sized `Copy` value with no destructor of its own ..., `nullable` as an `Option` of it" — nothing says whether a parameter of a handle type is a pointer contract, so `device: borrowed` in the document's own overlay is either accepted or `E5012` by `[FFI-11a]` ("A pointer contract with no count word is `E5012`"), since `[FFI-1]` counts "each pointer-typed parameter" and `VkDevice` is a pointer typedef in C; and "pointer-sized" is false for `VkBuffer` on a 32-bit target (`VK_DEFINE_NON_DISPATCHABLE_HANDLE`, a `uint64_t`), so the layout cannot be read from the rule (it is verified by `[FFI-5]`, which only makes the sentence a wrong fact). The reader's edit is right on both, but its clause "it takes no word but `nullable`, and a pointer word on it is `E5002`" removes the ownership words from handle slots, which the text relies on: `[FFI-8]` itself says "`destroys(f)` applies to an `owns T` of its type", and `[FFI-33b]` "`returns_owned` results and callbacks may carry `threads(creator)`: an `owns T` foreign value of such a type is two words ... the rule that makes GPU, GL-context and COM handles safe to hold in ordinary values" — an `owns T` of a handle type comes from `returns_owned(destructor=f)` on a handle result and goes to `owns` on a handle parameter. The better text refuses the count, lifetime, aliasing and `borrowed` words (a handle is passed by value) and keeps `nullable`, `owns` and `returns_owned(destructor=f)`. The example and `[FFI-11]` edits stand.

better_edits.old:
A `handle` is an opaque pointer-sized `Copy` value with
  no destructor of its own (`destroys(f)` applies to an `owns T` of its type, never to the handle),
  `nullable` as an `Option` of it, and bound to its thread under `threads(creator)` (`[FFI-33b]`,
  `E7008`).
better_edits.new:
A `handle` is an opaque `Copy` value with the C type's representation (a pointer or an integer:
  Vulkan's `VkBuffer` is a `uint64_t` on 32-bit targets), passed and returned by value and never
  read through, with no destructor of its own (`destroys(f)` applies to an `owns T` of its type,
  never to the handle), `nullable` as an `Option` of it (the null pointer or zero is `None`), and
  bound to its thread under `threads(creator)` (`[FFI-33b]`, `E7008`). A parameter or result of a
  handle type is no pointer contract: it is passed by value, so a count, lifetime or aliasing word
  or `borrowed` on it is `E5002` ("`device` is a `VkDevice`, a `handle` passed by value; remove
  `borrowed`"); it takes `nullable`, and the ownership words where the call transfers the handle's
  object, `returns_owned(destructor=f)` on a result and `owns` on a parameter, which give and take an
  `owns T` of the handle type (`[FFI-33b]`, two words under `threads(creator)`).
better_edits.why: The reader's definition with the ownership words kept: `[FFI-8]`'s own `destroys(f)` sentence and `[FFI-33b]`'s GPU handles need an `owns T` of a handle type, which `returns_owned` and `owns` produce.

A C host ends an object given with `into_raw()` with `ember_rt_object_release(void*)` (`[FFI-27]`), on an attached thread, which does what its last owner's end would

C gives a foreign object back through `adopt` inside `unsafe:` (`[FFI-36a]`). An `ObjectPtr[C]` is the address of a class object, which `into_raw()` gives, with no count of its own (to C, one pointer): `Copy`, equal when it is the address of the same object.
A C++ function returning a raw pointer with no ownership contract yields `*mut T`; `ffi.adopt[T](p)` (`unsafe`) turns it into an `owns T` ended through the contract's destructor.

`std.ffi.adopt[T](h) -> owns T` is an `unsafe fn` that takes ownership of a foreign object, reading its destructor from the contract of `T`'s declaration, `@ffi(destroys(f))` on `type T`; the `owns T` value's end calls `f` once.

A function returning an opaque class by value gives an `owns T`, as a constructor does: the result is moved to an object of its own, ended by the class's destructor; an abstract class, or one without a public destructor, is refused (ODR-166).

The hole is real. CLS-4 decides replacement by name alone: "A method named like an inherited one replaces it (ODR-028): over a virtual method without `override` it is `E2111`, and over a non-virtual one it is `E2110`, `override` or not"; DSP-2: "an `override` reuses the base's slot"; the only signature rule for overrides is FFI-39's `E5056`, for a C++ base. So `override fn on(e: KeyEvent)` fills `Handler.on(e: Event)`'s slot and `send(log, MouseEvent(x=3))` reads a `MouseEvent` as a `KeyEvent` from safe code: type confusion PHIL-10 forbids. It cannot be forged: TYP-7 "`as` between pointer types, or between a pointer and an integer, requires `unsafe`", and `null[P]()` takes a raw-pointer type ("`P` must be a raw-pointer type"), not a callable type. So `TICK_ROM_HANDLER` is the header's own address, and C calling it is "a bug in foreign code reached through a correctly declared boundary" or the header's intent (PHIL-11), not a pointer safe code chose; and `fire=None` is writable only where the field's type is `Option`, which the importer gives only "when nullable". That differs from a raw pointer, which `null[P]()`, `ref_to_ptr` and `as_ptr()` make in safe code. The reader's clause for "a value of an `unsafe` callable type held so" would refuse every safe entry taking a hook table filled with C's or Ember's own functions (`VkAllocationCallbacks`, SDL, cJSON) and buy nothing; it is dropped from the FFI-10 edit (NG-37). What the cluster does show is left unsaid: how an imported struct's function-pointer field becomes `Option` (listed under missed).

The hole is real: FFI-17a gives `CppVector[T]` "with `.span()`, `.span_mut()`, `.to_array()`, `push_back`, `len`" as safe bridge operations, §IV.5 makes `null[P]()` safe, FFI-40 makes the `const std::vector<const char*>&` a plain `names: CppVector[*c_char]`, and the entry asserts the call safe with no fact about the elements (FFI-1's facts attach to "pointer-typed parameter and result" only). C++ calls `puts(nullptr)` from safe code. The reader's FFI-10 edit reaches it through "an element of … a bridge type (`CppVector[T]`, `[FFI-17a]`)", and a `CppVector[Mesh]` of a pointer-free struct keeps its safe entry. Narrowed only to apply the FFI-10 text in NG-37's better form (the `unsafe`-callable clause dropped, the result sentence made consistent).

better_edits.old: A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`.
better_edits.new: A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`. The same holds for a raw pointer held inside a parameter at any depth, as the parameter's Ember type declares it: a field of a `@layout(c)` value type, an element of a fixed array or of a bridge type (`CppVector[T]`, `[FFI-17a]`), the payload of an `Option`, the pointee of a contracted pointer, a value passed by a C++ reference (`[FFI-40]`). Safe code may set such a field or element to a pointer nothing checks (`null[P]()`, `ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), so no declaration asserts a call that carries one to foreign code safe: `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` (`[GRM-35]`, `[FFI-2]`), `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef (`[FFI-56]`) and `@ffi(std_function, safe)` (`[FFI-17a]`) with one are `E5002`, naming the field or element ("`count_spaces`'s `s.p` is a raw pointer, which safe code may point anywhere, so no call of `count_spaces` can be safe; write `unsafe fn count_spaces(s)` with `@safety(\"`s.p` points at `s.n` readable bytes\")` above it, and build the `Slice` inside an `unsafe:` block of a wrapper that takes `text: Span[u8]`"). A raw pointer held inside a result or an `out` value, which foreign code set, is not refused: reading through it is `unsafe` already (`[UNS-1]`), and a call that carries it back to foreign code is judged by this sentence where that call's function is declared.
better_edits.why: The same FFI-10 text as NG-37.

verdicts.reason: The hole is real on the reading that accepts `ref mut BufDesc` in a callback type (unsaid; FFI-21 says only "its body is checked as an export under `threads=any` is" and FFI-31b lowers "`ref mut x: T` as `T*`" for exports), and under it `d.data = ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` is a safe store (UNS-1 fences a write "through `*T`/`*mut T`", not a store of a pointer value) that FFI-21a never sees (`fill` returns nothing). C writes 4,096 bytes into `fill`'s dead frame (FFmpeg's `get_buffer2` shape). The reader's FFI-21a rewrite has the provenance leaks given under NG-32; the UNS-1 entry decides it by the operation: a store of a raw pointer into "a `ref mut` or `MutSpan` parameter of such a function, or a field of one" is `E3100` with the block to write. Whether an `extern "C" fn` type may carry `ref mut` at all is listed under missed.

better_edits.old: access a foreign `static mut` (`[STA-1]`);
better_edits.new: access a foreign `static mut` (`[STA-1]`); give foreign code a raw pointer, as `into_raw()` does: return a raw pointer, or a value holding one at any depth, from a function foreign code may call (one whose value becomes an `extern "C" fn`, `[FN-6]`, `[FFI-21]`; an export or an `@export_table` field's function, `[FFI-26]`; an `override fn` of a C++ virtual method, `[FFI-39]`: the functions `[FFI-52]` lists), or store one into a place foreign code reads with no call Ember sees (a `ref mut` or `MutSpan` parameter of such a function, or a field of one; a place reached through the `ref mut` view a foreign result's lifetime word gives, `[FFI-11]`, `[FFI-40]`; a foreign `static mut`), since safe code may make a pointer that is null, dangling or shorter than a count beside it (§IV.5, `[SPN-8]`) and code nothing checks reads it there (`E3100`: "`spare` returns `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` (line 7) to C, which uses the pointer after `spare` has returned; put line 7 in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note saying why C may use it"); a pointer into a parameter C passes as a copy stays refused outright (`E5042`, `[FFI-21a]`);
better_edits.why: The same edit as NG-32.

verdicts.reason: The text decides it, safely. THR-2: "A line that makes a value `thread_shared` (`t = thread_shared Tree(items=[item])`, `[THR-1]`), and a store under a lock into a field of one (`t.items.push(owns item)`, `[THR-18]`), makes every class object the stored value owns reachable from any thread, and is such a hand-over for each of them: the compare is made there, so a `weakref T` link made before it (`w = weakref item`) finds its object ended afterwards, and no plain weak count is ever touched from two threads." Line 31, `log = thread_shared Log(results=Mutex([fail(owns e)]))`, is such a line; the walk "follows the handed value's fields and elements by their types, through `owns` blocks, `Option`s and collections" to `AnyError`'s "`owns dyn Error`" (ERR-8), and "an object held `dyn I` … is walked by the hand-over routine its own package compiled beside its `drop`". `LoadError` carries the weak count by OBJ-1 ("or when a `weakref` type in the package names it"), so the compare runs, the old block is marked ended, WK-12's `else:` path runs ("a target handed to another thread is ended here, `[THR-2]`") and the program prints `done`. The finder tested a proposed change's cost line, not the current text, which already lists the `thread_shared` line among the hand-overs.

Decided by THR-15 as rewritten under ruling N80: "`Sender[T]` and `Receiver[T]` are `Send`, and `Sender[T]` is `ThreadShared`, exactly when `T` is `Send` (`[THR-8]`), so a one-thread owner never crosses through a channel: an end of a channel of such a `T` given to another thread is `E7015` at that line, as any value that is not `Send` (`[THR-2]`)." `shares Doc` is a one-thread owner (THR-8: "nothing reachable from it … is a one-thread owner (`shares T`, `shares mut T`)"), so `Receiver[shares Doc]` is not `Send` and `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: consume(rx))` is `E7015` at that line. The finder's complaint was about a change's impact column quoting the old THR-15; the current text says what the column claimed. The refusal is safe.

The current text decides the program one way, and safely: ERR-9 "The error parameter defaults to `AnyError`", ERR-8 "a `dyn Error` held alone (`owns dyn Error`)", THR-8 "`dyn I` when `I` requires it (`interface I: needs Send:`)" and ERR-3's `Error` as "`Display + Debug` with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]`", which requires no marker, so `AnyError` is not `Send`; THR-15 then makes `Sender[Result[int]]` not `Send`, and THR-10's "a function that holds a one-thread value is `E7015`" refuses `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: produce(tx))`. The clash the finder quoted between the old THR-15 and THR-8 is gone (N80). The refusal is safe; that it is needless for an ordinary program is K20's open question (whether `Error` requires the markers), outside this cluster, and K20's record itself depends on NG-25's hole being closed first.

Not a defect of the specification. TXT-10 fixes `ParseError`'s shape only: "`ParseError`, in `std.string`, is a unit-only enum, `Empty`, `Invalid` or `Overflow`, naming the first problem from the left"; FN-8 fixes how `main`'s error is printed ("An `Err` returned from `main` is printed with `Display` to standard error and the process exits with status 1"); DRV-1's `Display` row applies to a derived `Display`, and nothing says `ParseError`'s is derived. The text `the text is not a value of this type` is std's (`std/src/string.em`), which the document leaves to the library as it does every std error text but ERR-4's `called unwrap on None`. The finder's advice (assert a code, or a text the program itself fixes through `AnyError.msg(...)` or an `@error("…")` of its own) needs no rule; fixing std's texts in the document would be a std-reference question for every error type, not this one.

The status is right: the current text decides the program, memory-safely. RC-4 point 3 places check points "at every loop's back edge, before and after every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, a `join`, the end of a `with scope` block, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends", and point 5 says plainly "it is ended at its making thread's next check point. Until then it is intact"; so the `Buffer` is freed when `stop.recv()` returns, and the program's own spin on `FREED` is what hangs it, a deadlock PHIL-11 lists outside the guarantee. The finder measured the text against the K10 design's wake for job workers, which is in no rule of the current text. The reader's edits should not be applied alone: (1) their safety premise, "where the queued drops were already judged as the point's own (`[THR-19]`, `[THR-20]`)", is not in the text (THR-19 and THR-20 say nothing of a check point's queued drops; that judgment is exactly what the K10 design adds and what its arbiter sent back over E3-1), so the edit imports one piece of a rejected design without the piece that makes drops at a point safe to run; (2) it is a run-time addition that changes the shape of every blocking call (a wait that the queue can interrupt, a loop of wait, empty, wait again) beyond the one wake its §X.4 row names; (3) K10's own decision chose the wake for job workers only, and widening it is K10's revision to weigh. Verdict 101 ("That thread deletes it at its next check point") is consistent with either. Carry the finding into K10; apply nothing here.

The same as NG-46. RC-4 points 3 and 5 decide the program: main's `Session`, which "travelled inside another object", "is ended at its making thread's next check point. Until then it is intact", and main's next point is after `h.join()` ("before and after every call that may block the thread (… a `join` …)"), so `CLOSED` stays 0 while `serve` spins on it: the program's own deadlock (PHIL-11). The finder's "special case" is K10's design, absent from the text. The reader's wake edits are not to be applied alone, for the three reasons given under NG-46 (a safety premise the text does not hold, a run-time reshaping of every blocking call beyond the named cost, and K10's own scope decision); their general form (every waiting thread woken) is the right question for K10's revision, where its E3-1 objection (which thread's function counts the last drops) must be settled with it.

missed.title: The parameter words an `extern "C" fn` type may carry are unsaid
missed.rules: FN-6: "A function that captures nothing also coerces to `extern "C" fn(…)` when every type is FFI-safe"; FFI-21: "its body is checked as an export under `threads=any` is (`[FN-6]`, `[FFI-33]`)"; FFI-31b: "An export's parameters and result are written in the safe types of `[FFI-10]`'s mapping and lowered to the same carriers: … `ref mut x: T` as `T*`". FFI-31b names the set and the carriers for an export's signature only; FN-6 says "FFI-safe" without naming the set; FFI-21 maps a callback's parameters from the C pointer type "a raw pointer among them staying raw", which a hand declaration has no C type to map from. So NG-32's `extern "C" fn(usize, ref mut *mut u8)` and NG-41's `extern "C" fn(ref mut BufDesc)` are accepted on one reading (lowered as an export's `T*`) and `E2020` on another, and two compilers disagree.

edits.old: A function that captures nothing also coerces to `extern "C" fn(…)` when every type is FFI-safe;
edits.new: A function that captures nothing also coerces to `extern "C" fn(…)` when every type is FFI-safe: its parameters and result are those `[FFI-31b]` admits in an export's signature, written with the same words and lowered to the same carriers (`ref mut x: T` as `T*`, `Span[T]` as a pointer and a `size_t`), and any other is `E2020`, naming the parameter;
edits.why: FN-6 is where the coercion is granted; naming the set once by the export rule that already lists it decides every hand-declared callback type and every `@layout(c)` function-pointer field the same way.

missed.title: How an imported struct's function-pointer field becomes `Option`
missed.rules: FFI-56: "A function pointer that comes from C — a field of an imported struct, a typedef, a result, an `extern static`, an argument C passes to a callback — imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` (`Option[…]` when nullable, `[FN-6]`)"; FFI-30a: an overlay "never changes a type's identity, layout or fields"; FFI-11: the nullability word attaches to contracted pointer slots. No contract reaches a struct field, so "when nullable" names a fact no declaration can state for a field: an implementer cannot decide whether `timer_spec.fire` is `unsafe extern "C" fn(c_int)` (safe code can never store null; C's own null is a value invalid for its type, `[UNS-4]`) or `Option[unsafe extern "C" fn(c_int)]` (safe code may store `None`, and the struct reaches C through a safe entry).

edits.old: imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` (`Option[…]` when nullable, `[FN-6]`)
edits.new: imports as `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` (`Option[…]` when its slot's contract says `nullable`, `[FFI-11]`; a field of an imported struct, which no contract reaches (`[FFI-30a]`), is always the `Option`, since C may leave it null and safe code must be able to read what C wrote)
edits.why: The one place the nullable form is granted; a field has no contract, so the rule must decide it itself, and the `Option` is the only form that keeps `[UNS-4]`'s 'every value is valid for its type' true for a struct C filled.

missed.title: The move a `T&&` override makes is a thunk operation `ember inspect` should list
missed.rules: FFI-17f: "`ember inspect` reports each bridge operation that is a thunk call rather than an inlined one (`CppShared` clone and drop, `CppVector` `push_back`, `len` and drop, `CppString` drop, a `std_function` value's drop, and the conversion of a `std::optional` or `std::variant` at a call)"; PHIL-15: "Every cost the language can insert without the programmer writing it … has a row in §X.4 and is reported per site by `ember inspect`". With NG-29's edit the trampoline runs `T`'s move constructor before an `override fn take(owns p: T)` runs, and the thunk runs `T`'s destructor on the moved-from object after a call from Ember to a `T&&` parameter; neither is in FFI-17f's list.
missed.program:
class Counter(jb.jobs.Sink):
    bytes: c_int = 0
    override fn take(owns p: jb.jobs.Payload):   # one move constructor of `Payload` per call, inserted by the trampoline
        this.bytes += p.size()

edits.old: a `std_function` value's drop, and the conversion of a `std::optional` or `std::variant` at a call).
edits.new: a `std_function` value's drop, the conversion of a `std::optional` or `std::variant` at a call, the move constructor a trampoline runs for a `T&&` parameter of an `override fn` and the destructor of the moved-from object after a call from Ember to a `T&&` parameter (`[FFI-40]`)).
edits.why: PHIL-15: a cost the language inserts is reported per site; this one is new with NG-29's edit.

missed.title: An interface implementation's method need not have the interface's first line
missed.rules: IFC-1: "`extend T:` without `implements` adds inherent methods to `T`"; IFC-3: "`interface Ord: needs Eq` requires implementers of `Ord` to implement `Eq`"; IFC-4: an associated type "with a value that meets them (`E2040` if it is missing or does not)"; DSP-3: "Each entry of an interface's table holds, beside the implementation's code, the fact `[LT-22]` records for it, in the width the interface's declaration fixes". No rule says an `extend T implements I` writes each method with the parameter words, types and result `I` declares (the K11 critic's note records the gap: "needs a rule that an interface implementation's signature must match, which J5's notes found missing"); a call through `dyn I` passes what the interface declared into code that reads something else, the same confusion as NG-30 for `virtual`.
missed.program:
interface Scaler:
    fn scale(k: f64) -> f64

struct Sq:
    side: f64

extend Sq implements Scaler:
    fn scale(k: i64) -> f64:          # not the interface's first line; no rule refuses it
        return this.side * (k as f64)

fn apply(s: dyn Scaler) -> f64:
    return s.scale(2.5)               # the table's entry runs `Sq.scale` reading the `f64` bits as an `i64`

fn main():
    println(apply(Sq(side=2.0)))

edits.new: An implementation writes each of the interface's methods with the interface's first line after the name: the same parameter names, words and types, the same words on `this` and the same result, since a call through `dyn I` (`[DSP-3]`) passes what the interface declared; one that differs is `E2040`, naming the method and the interface's line ("`Sq.scale` takes `k: i64`, and `Scaler.scale` takes `k: f64`; write `fn scale(k: f64) -> f64:`").
edits.why: The same hole as NG-30 for the second table of `[LT-48]`; IFC-3 is where what an implementation promises its interface is stated, so the sentence goes there once for every interface (the lead may place it where `extend T implements I` is checked, if that rule has another id).

rulings.title: May a safe C or C++ call take a struct that holds raw pointers, and what limits raw pointers under the safe-to-call fact?

designs.question: K07: May a safe C or C++ call take a struct that holds raw pointers, and what limits raw pointers under the safe-to-call fact? (J8-08; angle: speed first, then safety.)
designs.summary: No. The safe-to-call fact ([FFI-2]) gets one limit, stated where the fact is defined and shared by every spelling that asserts it (`safe fn`, a plain overlay function entry, `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef, and `safe` beside `std_function`): no assertion covers a raw pointer that the call carries to foreign code, whether it is the argument itself, is held at any depth by what an argument passes (a field, a union field, an element, a C++ method's object, read from the Ember type), or is the result of a function-pointer type among them (what an Ember callback returns to C); such an assertion is `E5002` where it is written, and the function is `unsafe fn` with `@safety`, with an `extend` wrapper that builds the struct from a checked view inside `unsafe:`. The std_function contradiction that blocked the method-4 team is closed by giving the imported `std::function` the exact shape of [FFI-56]'s C function pointer: with `@ffi(std_function)` alone its value is an `unsafe fn(A…) -> R`, and `@ffi(std_function, safe)` asserts the target safe to call under the same limit. Nothing runs while the program runs: the limit is a walk over declared types at compile time, and the wrapper emits the same stores and the same single call as the C it replaces.

edits.old: (`[FFI-23]`, `[FFI-54]`): the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer |
edits.new: (`[FFI-23]`, `[FFI-54]`): the entry is written `unsafe fn`, with a raw pointer (`[FFI-2]`'s limit) |
edits.why: The row said a plain entry's call 'stays unsafe' although [GRM-35] says a function entry 'asserts the function safe to call'; with the limit in [FFI-2], an entry whose call carries a raw pointer is refused unless written `unsafe fn`, so the row must say the written form (verdicts 130, 136: no line silently means unsafe).

edits.old:
and on a
  function-pointer typedef, `safe` (`[FFI-56]`). `@ffi(effects=[…])` states effects.
edits.new:
and on a
  function-pointer typedef or a `std_function` type entry, `safe` (`[FFI-56]`, `[FFI-17a]`). `@ffi(effects=[…])` states effects.
edits.why: The vocabulary table must list the one new place the existing word `safe` may stand; no new word is added (verdict 133: `unsafe` stays no contract word).

edits.old:
Supplying the facts, in an `@ffi(…)` attribute or an overlay (§XVI.4), makes the
  call safe.
edits.new:
Supplying the facts, in an `@ffi(…)` attribute or an overlay (§XVI.4), makes the
  call safe, within the limit on raw pointers below.
edits.why: Read alone the sentence promises that complete facts always make a call safe; the limit qualifies exactly this promise.

edits.new: No assertion of the fact — `safe fn` (`[FFI-10]`), an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` (`[GRM-35]`), `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef (`[FFI-56]`) or `@ffi(std_function, safe)` on a `std::function` type (`[FFI-17a]`) — covers a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`) that a call carries to foreign code: an argument itself; one held, at any depth, by what an argument passes, by value or behind a contracted pointer (`one`, `count(n)`, `fixed(N)`, `exclusive`, `owns`), a C++ method's object included, as its Ember type declares it (a field, a union's field, an element of a `[T; N]`, a `Span`, a `MutSpan`, an `Option` or a `CppVector`; an `extern type`, an opaque class, a `@ffi(handle)` type and a bridge type declare none, `[FFI-8]`, `[FFI-17e]`); and the result, itself or at any depth in it, of a function-pointer type among them, since that is what an Ember function given to the call returns to foreign code. Safe code can make a raw pointer that is null (`null[P]()`), that points at fewer elements than a count beside it says or at a value already ended (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or that holds a constant address (`[FFI-6a]`), and no contract reaches it (`[FFI-1]`, `[FFI-30a]`), so nothing checks one. An assertion of the fact for a function whose call would carry one is `E5002` where it is written, naming the path to the pointer (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `get_buf`'s result) and giving the lines that leave the call unsafe: `@safety("…")` above the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` (a hand declaration keeping its C ABI parameters, `[FFI-10]`), or the typedef's or type's entry without `safe`; and each call in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note, or a wrapper in an `extend` block (`[FFI-13]`) that builds the value from checked views inside `unsafe:`; for an entry of another package's overlay, that entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`). A message elsewhere that offers an assertion of the fact (`safe fn lib_step`, a `callback(…)` word, `@ffi(safe)`) offers it only where this limit allows it (`[DIA-25]`). A raw pointer foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's or an export's parameter) is outside the limit: reading or writing through it is unsafe code (§IV.5). Nothing runs while the program runs for this rule: the limit is read from the declared types.
edits.why: This is where the safe-to-call fact is defined and where every spelling that asserts it points; one limit here reaches all of them, so no list elsewhere can disagree. The reach is a property of types in the Ember-to-foreign direction, never of a program's shape, and it is decided by the package that compiles the declaration from the header, the overlay and the types it sees ([BLD-16]).

edits.old:
`@layout(c)` value type, or a pointer whose contract is complete (given with `@ffi(…)` on the
  declaration), `safe` on any other function being `E5002`, naming the fact that is missing; or
edits.new:
`@layout(c)` value type, or a pointer whose contract is complete (given with `@ffi(…)` on the
  declaration), within `[FFI-2]`'s limit on raw pointers, `safe` on any other function being `E5002`, naming the fact that is missing or where the raw pointer is held; or
edits.why: The hole showed in this list: 'a `@layout(c)` value type' let `PixelBuf` through, and for J8-08 no fact is missing, so the message clause must name the other cause.

edits.old:
A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a
  raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002`.
edits.new:
A raw `*T` can be declared for an unsafe call, but complete facts do not make a
  raw-pointer parameter or result safe to expose; `safe fn` with one is `E5002` (`[FFI-2]`'s limit, for a pointer that is the parameter or result itself).
edits.why: Makes the existing sentence the hand-declaration case of the one property instead of a second rule of its own.

edits.old: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type (`E5002` otherwise): an asserted fact, listed by
edits.new: scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type, within `[FFI-2]`'s limit on raw pointers (`E5002` otherwise): an asserted fact, listed by
edits.why: The typedef's list grants a permission that would otherwise contradict [FFI-2]'s refusal of `@ffi(safe) type mix_fn` whose struct parameter holds `float* samples`.

edits.old: a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` (`[CLO-3]`) which owns its target, a foreign function: for `[EFF-2]` and `[CLO-17]`
