designs.runtime_cost: Nothing. The limit is a walk over declared types when the declaration is compiled; no instruction is emitted for it, and the §X.4 row "FFI call | guaranteed present | one direct call for an ABI-direct C function" is unchanged. The wrapper fills the struct from the span's pointer and length, the stores C itself writes to build the struct, and makes the same single call ([FFI-9]); after inlining it is the same instructions as the direct C call (a cross-package wrapper not inlined costs one extra call, as [FFI-29c] already prices a shim, removed by LTO, [BLD-FFI-4]). A `std::function` value's call keeps its thunk; `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` against `fn(A…) -> R` changes no code. To measure: `clear(ref mut frame)` against a hand-written C call with the same pointer and length, both compilers, same flags; expected identical time and code size.
designs.implementer_steps:
1. Add one predicate over Ember types, memoized per type: `carries_raw_pointer_to_foreign(T)`: true for `*T`/`*mut T`; for a `@layout(c)` struct or union, true if any field is; for `[T; N]`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `Option[T]`, `CppVector[T]`, `CppShared[T]` and any other type argument that names what a value holds or points at, true if the argument is; for a function-pointer type (`extern "C" fn(P…) -> R`, `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`), true if `R` is (the parameters `P…` are the C-to-Ember direction and are not walked); false for scalars, `@repr` enums, `CStrView`, `extern type`, opaque C++ classes, `@ffi(handle)` types, `CppString` and every type that declares no fields (cycles through pointers end at the pointer itself).
2. At each site that asserts the safe-to-call fact — a hand `safe fn` ([FFI-10]), an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` (a class member's entry includes its object type, [FFI-40]), `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef ([FFI-56]), `@ffi(std_function, safe)` on a type entry ([FFI-17a]) — run the predicate over each parameter's Ember type as the contract maps it (the pointee for `one`, `count(n)`, `fixed(N)`, `exclusive`, `owns`, `nullable`), and, for a C++ method, over the object's type; on a hit, emit `E5002` at the assertion with the first path found (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `get_buf`'s result) and the per-spelling fix lines. Keep [FFI-10]'s existing raw-pointer-slot refusal as the degenerate case (depth zero).
3. Import `std::function` with `@ffi(std_function)` as a value of type `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` (the existing owned-callable lowering, destructor thunk and [EFF-2]/[FFI-52] treatment unchanged); with `safe` in the same `@ffi(…)` run step 2 and give `fn(A…) -> R`. Record the `safe` assertion for `ember tcb`'s C++ bridge section.
4. The registry row of `E5002` gets the new cause; `ember bind --init` and `--check/--report` call the same predicate so a declaration the limit keeps from being safe is written and counted `unsafe fn`; messages that offer `safe fn`, a `callback(…)` word or `@ffi(safe)` consult the predicate first and omit the offer when it would be refused ([DIA-25]).
5. Tests: the refused program above (break-test: remove the predicate call, see it compile); the accepted program printing `[0, 0, 0, 0]`; the overlay, `@ffi(safe)` typedef, callback-result and `std_function` variants; `vkCmdSetViewport` and a `count(n)` span of `handle` values still safe; a C-returned struct with a pointer field read in `unsafe:` still accepted; a `std_function` without `safe` called outside `unsafe:` is `E3100`.
Separate compilation and hot reload need nothing new: the predicate reads only the header, the overlay and the declared types the compiling package sees ([BLD-16]); a changed overlay entry changes only Ember code ([HR-23]), and the call sites it turns unsafe are recompiled as any changed Ember code is.
designs.departs_from_verdict: None. Verdict 60 (anything that can break a safety promise only inside `unsafe`): applied, the route is closed. Verdicts 120, 125, 130, 133, 136: every refused assertion becomes `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn`, in a hand declaration, an overlay entry or a C++ member's entry, and no plain line silently means unsafe (the plain overlay entry is refused where it is written, not quietly made unsafe). Verdict 132's lesson (an unwritten attribute never falls back to an inferred fact): a plain overlay line keeps its written meaning and is refused when that meaning cannot hold. Verdict 137: results are outside the limit, not touched. Verdict 121: an entry of another package's overlay that the limit refuses fails every build that applies it, with the `override` line for the importing package. Verdict 73 / [DIA-25]: every fix line the message gives compiles, and messages elsewhere stop offering an assertion the limit refuses. Delegated rulings kept: ODR-073 (its reason, 'a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer', is the limit's reason, applied to a pointer in a field, an element or a callback result), ODR-074 (an unsafe hand declaration keeps its C ABI parameters), ODR-075 (`ref_to_ptr` stays safe; only handing the pointer to foreign code under an assertion of safety is refused), ODR-199 (`@ffi(std_function)` still makes an owned callable value; only its call's safety axis is now written, as [FFI-56] writes a C function pointer's). The std_function change touches no owner verdict; it is reported as the one change that refuses programs 0.9.20_Hardened_2 accepts (a call of a `std_function` value outside `unsafe:` without `safe` on the entry), in the spirit of §H.52 (every change of 0.9.20 is a refusal).
designs.trade_offs: Speed: nothing is given up; the limit costs no instruction and the wrapper is the C code's own stores and call, which is why this design is preferred over any run-time check (none could establish a pointer's validity anyway). Safety: closed at compile time for every type that carries a pointer and every route by which a call's arguments reach foreign code, including a callback's result and a `std::function` target; the dual route, an Ember export or an `override fn` of a C++ virtual that returns a raw pointer made in safe code, is outside the safe-to-call fact and is named under remaining doubt. Readability: a program that calls a binding gets a shorter line (`clear(ref mut frame)`); a binding author writes one `unsafe fn` entry with `@safety` and one wrapper per function whose structs carry pointers, the price Rust binding authors pay too, heaviest for Vulkan where every create-info has `pNext`. A program that only passes back to C a struct C itself returned (a camera frame with its pixel pointer) is refused as a safe call too, since the limit reads types, not who filled the field; the binding keeps such a struct in a private field of an Ember type behind a wrapper. Field contracts (an overlay stating `pQueueFamilyIndices: count(queueFamilyIndexCount)`) would let some such structs become safe types, but [FFI-30a] rules out an overlay touching fields, `pNext` chains could never be contracted, and it is a whole feature; not proposed. Consistency: one property in one rule, cited by the four lists that assert the fact; the `retained` row stops contradicting [GRM-35]; `std::function` follows the nearest rule ([FFI-56]) with existing words. Cost of the std_function change: existing programs calling a `std_function` value outside `unsafe:` must add `safe` to the entry (refused by the limit when the arguments carry a raw pointer) or move the call into `unsafe:`; `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites nothing, as for every 0.9.20 refusal.
designs.remaining_doubt: 1. The dual route is not closed by this ruling and is the same class of hole: an Ember function that foreign code calls — an `@unsafe(export(…))` function ([FFI-26], [FFI-31b] lists no refusal of a raw-pointer result), an `override fn` of a C++ virtual ([FFI-39], an `uint8_t* get_buf(size_t)` virtual) — may return `ref_to_ptr(ref mut local)` in safe code, and C or C++ writes through it. [FFI-21a] covers only a pointer into a copied parameter (`E5042`). The general shape, for K08's lead: a function foreign code calls whose result carries a raw pointer is written `unsafe fn` with `@safety`, so its body is unsafe code (verdict 118) and the author vouches for what the pointer points to and how long. 2. [FFI-11]'s `nullable` `Option[T]` input and `borrowed one nullable` carriers: the walk into `T` is stated in the limit; the implementer must apply the contract mapping before the walk, not the raw C type, so a `handle` behind `nullable` stays safe. 3. Whether `@ffi(std_function, safe)` should also carry [FFI-56]'s list ('every parameter and result is a scalar or a `@layout(c)` value type') or allow bridge types (`CppString`, `CppVector[T]` without pointers) as this ruling does; the limit refuses the raw pointers either way, and the narrower list would only refuse more correct programs. 4. The `vkCreateBuffer` rewrite must be merged with K46's edit of `device: borrowed` on the same lines; the `@safety` text given here is a proposal for the lead to shorten.

Safe code makes such a value null (`null[P]()`, `None`), one that outlives what it points at or counts fewer elements than a length beside it says (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or one holding any address (a pointer-cast constant, `[FFI-6a]`; a function pointer C handed back), and no contract word reaches it: words attach to parameters and results only (`[FFI-11]`), and no overlay touches a field (`[FFI-30a]`). The check reads the declaration and the header's types, which every package importing the header sees alike (`[FFI-30a]`), never the program (`[BLD-16]`), and nothing runs for it. A value foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter, a field of what it returns) is outside this limit: reading through it is unsafe (`[UNS-1]`), and `[FFI-10]` decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result.

The reason is ODR-073's ('a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer; the contract cannot establish validity'), which is about any assertion of safety, not about parameter slots. The trigger 'asserts the fact' keeps every entry whose own words already leave its calls unsafe (an unknown fact, an uncontracted raw-pointer slot, `retained` on a plain pointer, a `TODO(…)` word) exactly as today. C function pointers are in the property for the same reason as data pointers (NG-16/NG-18 of the gap sweep): a hook table whose `release` field safe code filled from a constant or from another library is code C calls with arguments nothing checks, while a safe `extern "C" fn` made from an Ember function is checked and never matches the limit's types.

designs.accepted_program:
```ember
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`buf.data` points at `buf.len` writable bytes")
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]):
    # SAFETY: `data` and `len` are the span's own pointer and length, so C writes exactly the bytes `bytes` views
    unsafe:
        clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=bytes.as_mut_ptr(), len=bytes.len()))

fn main():
    frame: [u8; 4] = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    clear(ref mut frame)           # a `[u8; 4]` given with `ref mut` converts to `MutSpan[u8]` ([SPN-1])
    println(frame[0], frame[3])    # 0 0
```

Safe callers can only clear bytes they own: `clear(ref mut frame)` is shorter than filling the struct by hand, and the one `unsafe:` block sits in the binding under its `# SAFETY:` note. The hand declaration keeps its C ABI parameters (an unsafe declaration is never mapped, [FFI-10]: "An unsafe raw-pointer declaration keeps its written C ABI parameters"), `ember tcb` lists the `unsafe:` block, and `L3015` never fires because `@safety` is written (verdict 120).

The `std::function` of the refused program, with the C function pointer's rule:

```ember
# overlays/fill.em
unsafe overlay cpp "fill.hpp":
    @ffi(std_function)
    type Fill
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    fn make_filler()

# main.em
import cpp "fill.hpp" with (project="fill", overlay="overlays/fill.em") as f

fn zero(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8], fill: f.px.Fill):
    # SAFETY: the struct describes exactly the bytes `bytes` views, and the target writes `len` bytes from `data`
    unsafe:
        fill(f.px.Buf(data=bytes.as_mut_ptr(), len=bytes.len()))

fn main():
    filler = f.px.make_filler()
    frame: [u8; 2] = [7, 7]
    zero(ref mut frame, filler)
    println(frame[0])              # 0
```

A `std::function<int(int)>` whose entry says `@ffi(std_function, safe)` stays a plain `fn(int) -> int`, called anywhere, as today.
designs.runtime_cost: Nothing. The limit is decided when the declaration, overlay entry or typedef is compiled, from types the compiler already has; no instruction is emitted for it (§X.4 row "Contract and range-type annotations | not observable | compile time only"). The call that replaces the refused safe call is the same one direct call (§X.4 row "FFI call | guaranteed present | one direct call for an ABI-direct C function"); the wrapper fills the struct from the span's pointer and length, as C code fills it, and inlines to the same instructions. A `std_function` value's call is unchanged (one call through the owned target and the thunk FFI-17f already reports); only the word `safe` on its entry changes where the call may be written.
designs.implementer_steps:
1. One predicate over Ember types, `carries_unchecked_pointer(ty) -> Option<path>`: a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`, `ObjectPtr[C]`) or an `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` type is a hit (path = the place); `Option[X]`, `[X; N]`, `Span[X]`, `MutSpan[X]`, a tuple, a `@layout(c)` struct or union, a generic bridge type (`CppVector[X]`) walk their fields, elements and type arguments (memoised per type; a pointer is a leaf, so the walk ends); a callable type walks its result only; an `extern type`, an opaque C++ class, a `@ffi(handle)` type, a `@ffi(newtype)` of a scalar and every scalar are misses. The path is a dotted name from the parameter (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `get_buf`'s result, `Buf.data` of parameter 1).
2. In the hand-declaration checker ([FFI-10]): for a `safe fn`, after the existing slot checks, run the predicate on every parameter's mapped Ember type (the value type behind `one`, `count(n)`, `owns`, `fixed(N)`; a `callback(…)` parameter's `fn(P…) -> R`); a hit is E5002 at the declaration with the new message (the `@safety` + `unsafe fn` line with the declaration's C ABI parameters, the call lines that need `unsafe:`, and the wrapper hint when the hit is a data pointer).
3. In the importer's overlay binder ([GRM-35], [FFI-2]): for every function entry not written `unsafe fn` (a class section's methods included, with the class type as the object), run the predicate on each parameter's produced Ember type and on the receiver; E5002 at the entry, with the `override` form in the message when the overlay belongs to another package ([FFI-30c]). For a typedef entry with `safe` ([FFI-56]) and a type entry with `std_function, safe` ([FFI-17a]): run it on each parameter of the pointed-to or wrapped signature.
4. `@ffi(std_function)`: the type of the value is `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` unless the entry carries `safe`; the existing `unsafe` callable machinery ([FN-6], ODR-115, [UNS-1]) then refuses calls outside `unsafe:` with E3100, whose text FFI-17a gives, adding the `safe` line only when step 3's predicate would pass for the entry (so the message's line compiles, [DIA-25], and `unsafe` is not suggested while a fix without it compiles, [DIA-9]).
5. `ember bind --init` ([CLI-5]): run the predicate while writing each entry; a hit writes `unsafe fn` with a `@safety("TODO")` line, so the starter compiles unchanged. `ember tcb` lists `safe` on a `std_function` entry beside `@ffi(safe)` typedefs ([TCB-1]).
6. Registry and tests: the new E5002 cause and the FFI-17a E3100 text in the code tables; a conformance test per spelling (hand `safe fn` with a struct field, an overlay entry, an `@ffi(safe)` typedef, a `std_function, safe` entry, a callback result, a C++ method on a `@layout(c)` class, a `CppVector[Buf]` argument), each failing without the predicate; a positive test that an `extern type` or `handle` field is not reached, and that the Vulkan example compiles as edited.
7. Nothing in code generation, the runtime, Annex B or the interface files changes: the check is per declaration from the header's types, which [FFI-30a] makes identical across packages, so a package compiled once decides the same in every program ([BLD-16]).
designs.departs_from_verdict: None. Verdicts touched, each kept: 31 (`@ffi(no_callbacks)` untouched; a forgotten word refuses, never crashes); 60 (closes a route by which safe code broke memory safety; the call now happens only inside `unsafe:`); 73 and [DIA-25] (every message gives both lines, the declaration's and the call's, so its fix runs into no second error); 118, 119 (the wrapper's `unsafe:` block is ordinary unsafe code); 120, 125 (the refused declaration or entry becomes `@safety` above `unsafe fn`, C++ members included); 121 (an entry refused in another package's overlay fails every build that applies it, as a drifted one does, and the message gives the `override` line, [FFI-30c]); 130, 133 (that spelling, and no new contract word: `safe` is FFI-56's existing word, `unsafe` stays no word of `@ffi(…)`); 132 and 136 (a plain overlay line keeps its meaning 'safe to call' and is refused where it cannot be made safe, never made silently unsafe by a header field the reader does not see; a `std_function` entry's safety is written, never inferred from the header); 137 (results stay outside the limit, read from the callee's code where there is one; a C function has none); 165 (untouched). Delegated rulings: ODR-073 (its reason is the limit's reason; the slot sentence kept word for word), ODR-074 (an unsafe hand declaration keeps its C ABI parameters, as the message shows), ODR-075 and ODR-076 (`ref_to_ptr` and `null[P]()` stay safe; only handing the result to foreign code under an assertion of safety is refused), ODR-115 (`unsafe fn(…) -> R` is the type a `std_function` value takes), ODR-199 (an `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` is still 'an owned callable value'; the default changes from safe to unsafe to call, which Hardened_2's FFI-17a already implied by making the target 'a foreign function' under FFI-2's 'never derived').
designs.trade_offs: Safety is kept whole: a pointer the caller supplied never reaches foreign code under an assertion of safety, by any route the call's arguments give it, and the same words decide every spelling, so there is no struct-shaped, element-shaped, object-shaped or callback-shaped way around [FFI-10]'s slot rule. Speed: nothing runs, and the wrapper is the same struct fill and one direct call C writes. Readability: the ordinary caller's line gets shorter (`clear(ref mut frame)`); the price falls on binding authors, who write one `unsafe fn` entry with `@safety` and one wrapper per function whose structs carry pointers (the price Rust binding authors pay), heaviest for Vulkan, where every create-info has `pNext`, and for hook tables and ops structs, whose function-pointer fields now count too; a hand binding also writes its raw form by hand, since an unsafe hand declaration is not mapped (ODR-074). `std::function` values are callable in safe code only when their entry says `safe`, one word, and C++ callables whose parameters carry pointers are callable only in `unsafe:`, never vouched; a `std::function` taking `std::span` cannot be vouched either (the `safe` list is FFI-56's plus the bridge types; a span is not one), a conservative choice that keeps the unsafe call. Given up: today's acceptance of such declarations and the safe-by-default `std_function` (both accepted programs that broke a promise, or derived a fact [FFI-2] says is never derived). Not taken: field contracts in overlays (a whole feature [FFI-30a] rules out), making a write of a pointer into a struct unsafe (the length beside it stays a plain number safe code changes, so the hole stays), and refusing `std_function` entries outright (drops a feature, against the owner's condition on the delegation).
designs.remaining_doubt: 1. Exports: an `@export` function, or a function coerced to `extern "C" fn`, that returns a raw pointer it made in safe code (`ref_to_ptr(ref mut local)`) hands C a dangling address with no `unsafe` anywhere; [FFI-21a] covers only a pointer into a copied parameter (E5042) and [FFI-31b] lists no raw-pointer result among the refused ones. The limit here reaches a callback's result given to a foreign call, not an export C calls on its own; that is K08's question (export arguments and results from C) and should take the same property (a value safe code supplies that names memory nothing checks). 2. Handles: FFI-8 makes a `handle` an opaque `Copy` value, so a handle field is outside the limit; if a pointer-cast macro constant of a handle type (`((HANDLE)-1)`, [FFI-6a]) can be written in safe code, a forged handle still reaches C through a struct, which K46 should settle (a constant of a handle type is a value of it, or needs `unsafe`). 3. A union field (`@layout(c, union) struct`) holding a pointer under one alternative is reached whatever alternative the caller means, which is conservative and right for safety but refuses a safe entry for a tagged-union API; a wrapper is the way out. 4. An integer field C treats as an address (`uintptr_t`) stays the declarer's assertion, as [FFI-2]'s own `free_addr(uintptr_t)` example is for a parameter; the limit does not and cannot reach it. 5. `ember bind --check` and `--report` ([CLI-6], [CLI-7]) count declarations as safe or unsafe without the limit; the compile refuses the entry, so no program is accepted, but the tools' counts may name an entry safe that the build refuses; a one-line cite there is cheap if the lead wants it. 6. The `@safety` text for `vkCreateBuffer` names Vulkan's own validity rules in prose; a reader of the example may want it shorter.

designs.question: K07: May a safe C or C++ call take a struct that holds raw pointers, and what limits raw pointers under the safe-to-call fact?
designs.summary: The rule a newcomer holds in one sentence: safe code never hands C an address it made up, so a C or C++ call is safe to make only when nothing the call gives foreign code holds a raw pointer, alone, in a struct, in a span's elements, in a C++ object, or returned by an Ember function the call gives C; a raw pointer reaches foreign code only from an `unsafe:` block, under a `@safety` someone wrote. The limit is stated once, in `[FFI-2]`, where the safe-to-call fact is defined, and every spelling that asserts the fact shares it: `safe fn`, a plain overlay function entry, `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef, and `safe` beside `std_function`; a `std::function` value is otherwise `unsafe fn(A…) -> R`, as a C function pointer already is under `[FFI-56]`, which removes the two-ways reading of `[FFI-17a]`. A refused declaration is `E5002` where it is written, naming the field that holds the pointer; the binding writes `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn` and one `extend` wrapper that fills the struct from a checked `MutSpan`, so callers write a shorter safe line and nothing runs while the program runs.

edits.new:

edits.why: Read alone, the sentence promises that complete facts always make a call safe; the cite keeps it true for a struct whose field no contract reaches ([FFI-1]: a contract is 'for each pointer-typed parameter and result'; [FFI-30a]: an overlay 'never changes a type's identity, layout or fields').

edits.rule: FFI-2 (append: the limit on raw pointers)
edits.new: Every spelling that asserts the fact — `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn`, and `safe` on a callable type's entry (`@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef, `[FFI-56]`; `@ffi(std_function, safe)` on a `std::function`'s, `[FFI-17a]`) — asserts it for calls that hand foreign code no raw pointer the caller supplied. A contract reaches a pointer-typed parameter or result and nothing else (`[FFI-1]`; an overlay never touches a type's fields, `[FFI-30a]`), and safe code may make a raw pointer that is null (`null[P]()`), that outlives what it points at or points at fewer elements than a count beside it says (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or that is a constant address (`[FFI-6a]`); so no assertion covers one. The raw pointers a call hands foreign code are read from the Ember types of what it passes: an argument that is one (`*T`, `*mut T`, `ObjectPtr[C]`); one held, at any depth, by a value an argument passes by value or behind a contracted pointer (`one`, `count(n)`, `owns`), in a field, an element, a union member or a type argument, a C++ method's object included; and one that an Ember function the call gives foreign code, as an argument or held by one, returns, itself or inside its result (a function value is not a raw pointer; what it returns is read). A declaration or entry in one of those spellings whose calls would hand one is `E5002` where it is written, naming where the pointer is held (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `get_buf`'s result) and the line that leaves the calls unsafe: `@safety("…")` above it written `unsafe fn` (a hand declaration with its C ABI parameters, `[FFI-10]`), or the type's entry without `safe`; each call then goes in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note (`[UNS-1]`), or behind an `extend` wrapper that fills the value from a checked view (`[FFI-13]`); for an entry in another package's overlay the line is an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`). A raw pointer foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter, a field of a value it returns) is outside this limit: reading or writing through it is unsafe code's already (`[UNS-1]`), and `[FFI-10]` decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result. A `@ffi(handle)` value (`[FFI-8]`), a `CStrView`, a `Span[T]` or `MutSpan[T]`, and an opaque type, which declares no field, are not raw pointers. The limit is read from the declarations the compiling package sees (`[BLD-16]`), and nothing runs for it while the program runs.
edits.why: This is where the safe-to-call fact is defined ('it is asserted by `safe fn` in an extern block (`[FFI-10]`), or by an overlay entry for the function, which asserts that a call within its contract cannot break memory safety'), and the fact has no limit: a raw pointer in a field is 'within its contract' because the contract never mentions it. ODR-073's reason (a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer) is a property of every assertion of the fact, so the limit sits above all four spellings instead of in each list. Naming the spellings closes the method-4 team's blocking objection (E2-1): the consequence sentence reaches exactly the spellings the first sentence names, and each has a line that compiles (DIA-25).

designs.refused_program:
```ember
# pixels.em — C: void clear_pixels(struct PixelBuf buf) writes buf.len zero bytes at buf.data
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

fn main():
    x: u8 = 7
    clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096))
    println(x)
```

Today every line is safe code and C writes 4,096 bytes over one. Under the ruling the program is refused at line 9:

`E5002`: "`clear_pixels` is declared `safe fn`, but `buf.data` is a raw pointer (`*mut u8`), which safe code may fill with any address, and `buf.len` with any count, and no contract reaches a field; write `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` saying what `buf.data` must point at, and put each call in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note, or give safe callers an `extend` wrapper that fills `PixelBuf` from a `MutSpan[u8]` inside `unsafe:`".

The same code and shape of message refuse: an overlay entry `fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)` whose header struct holds `const char* path` (naming `opts.path`, giving `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn cp_load(opts: borrowed one)`, or an `override` of it in the importing package's overlay); `@ffi(safe) type mix_fn` whose struct parameter holds `float* samples` (giving the entry without `@ffi(safe)`); `@ffi(std_function, safe) type Fill` for `std::function<void(Buf)>` with `uint8_t* data` in `Buf` (giving `@ffi(std_function) type Fill`, whose value is `unsafe fn(Buf)`); and `safe fn stream_read(want: usize, get_buf: fn(usize) -> *mut u8)` with `callback(borrowed)`, naming `get_buf`'s result.
designs.accepted_program:
```ember
# pixels.em — C: void clear_pixels(struct PixelBuf buf); void clear_bytes(uint8_t* data, size_t len)
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8
    len: usize

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`buf.data` points at `buf.len` bytes C may write during the call")
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

    # the same work with the pointer and count as parameters: a complete contract, safe as today ([FFI-10], ODR-074)
    @ffi(param(data, borrowed, count(len), exclusive), no_callbacks)
    safe fn clear_bytes(ref mut data: MutSpan[u8], len: usize)

fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]):
    # SAFETY: the struct describes exactly the bytes of `bytes`, which this call views `ref mut`, so C writes only them
    unsafe:
        clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=bytes.as_mut_ptr(), len=bytes.len()))

fn main():
    frame: Array[u8] = [7, 7, 7, 7]
    clear(ref mut frame)          # the struct is filled from a checked view; prints [0, 0, 0, 0]
    frame = [7, 7, 7, 7]
    clear_bytes(ref mut frame)    # `len` is the witness the compiler supplies; prints [0, 0, 0, 0]
    println(frame)
```

Safe callers can only clear bytes they own; `clear(ref mut frame)` is shorter than building the struct by hand. A C++ `std::function<void(int)>` mapped `@ffi(std_function, safe) type OnTick` stays a plain `fn(int)` value called from safe code, since an `int` is not a raw pointer; one mapped `@ffi(std_function)` alone is an `unsafe fn(…)` value, called inside `unsafe:` as a C function pointer is today.
designs.runtime_cost: Nothing. The limit is decided when compiling, from the declaration's types. The wrapper fills the struct from the span's pointer and length, as C code fills it, and makes the one direct call that §X.4's row "FFI call | guaranteed present | one direct call for an ABI-direct C function" already lists ([FFI-9]: "An ABI-direct call is one `call` instruction and nothing else"); after inlining the instructions are those of the C program. A `std::function` value's call and drop cost what [FFI-17f] already reports, whether the entry says `safe` or not. No row of §X.4 changes.
designs.implementer_steps:
1. In the FFI front end, after contract resolution and the mapping to Ember types ([FFI-10], [FFI-11], [FFI-8]), compute for each foreign callable declaration whether it asserts the safe-to-call fact: a hand `safe fn`; an overlay function entry (in or outside a class section) not written `unsafe fn`; a typedef entry carrying `@ffi(safe)`; a type entry carrying `@ffi(std_function, safe)`. Parse `safe` as a second word of `@ffi(std_function, …)` (the `@ffi(…)` word list already takes several words; `unsafe` stays `E0104`).
2. For an asserting declaration, walk the Ember-side type of everything the call hands foreign code: each parameter's mapped type (`x: T`, `ref mut x: T`, `Span[T]`/`MutSpan[T]`, `Option[…]`, `owns T`, `[T; N]`), a C++ method's class for `this`, and for a `callback(…)` parameter or an `extern "C" fn`-typed slot the callable type's result (never its parameters, which C supplies). The walk descends through `@layout(c)` struct and union fields, fixed-array and span elements, `Option` and tuple components, type arguments of generic and bridge types (`CppVector[Slice]`), and callable results, with a visited set over nominal types; it stops at scalars, `@ffi(handle)` types, `CStrView`, `extern type`s and opaque C++ classes (no declared fields), and bridge strings. Field types come from the `.embind`'s recorded declarations ([FFI-14]) or the extern block, so the package compiling the line sees everything it reads ([BLD-16]); no whole-program fact enters.
3. On reaching `*T`, `*mut T` or `ObjectPtr[C]`, record the access path (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `items[].pNext`, `get_buf()`'s result) and report `E5002` at the declaration or entry, with the fix line chosen by spelling: `@safety("…")` above the declaration written `unsafe fn` with its C ABI parameters (hand declaration; ODR-074's raw form), the same for an overlay entry, the typedef entry without `@ffi(safe)`, or the type entry without `safe`; for an entry applied from another package's overlay, the `override` line in the importing package's overlay ([FFI-30c]). One message per declaration, listing every path ([DIA-26]).
4. Type the `@ffi(std_function)` value `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` unless the entry says `safe`; the existing `unsafe fn(…)` callable machinery ([FN-6], [UNS-1]: `E3100` outside unsafe code) does the rest. `ember tcb` lists `@ffi(std_function, safe)` in the C++ bridge section.
5. `ember bind --init` runs the same walk and writes such declarations `unsafe fn` ([CLI-5]); `--check` and `--report` count them among the declarations still unsafe ([CLI-6], [CLI-7]). `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites nothing for this: the calls then need `unsafe:` (every 0.9.20 change is a refusal, N75).
6. Separate compilation: the check runs where the declaration is written and where an overlay is applied (as [FFI-55]'s drift check does); the interface file already carries each foreign function's safety, so dependants see the result. Hot reload: a reload image recompiles the package's declarations the same way ([BLD-16]), and a header change refuses the reload anyway ([HR-23]).
7. Tests: the refused program (E5002 at the `safe fn` line naming `buf.data`), the overlay, typedef, `std_function` and callback-result cases, the accepted wrapper program printing `[0, 0, 0, 0]`, the XVI.4 example compiling, and a break test with the walk disabled. Then the twin: time the wrapper `clear` against the direct C call with the same pointer and length under MSVC, clang and gcc; the expectation is identical instructions after inlining, reported with both code sizes.
designs.departs_from_verdict: None. Verdict 60 ("anything that can break a safety promise is possible only inside an `unsafe` block") is what the ruling enforces; verdicts 120, 125, 130 and 133 give the spelling of every fix line (`@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn`; `unsafe` never a word of `@ffi(…)`; `safe` is an existing contract word, [FFI-11]); verdict 132's lesson is kept (a plain overlay line is refused where it is written, never quietly made unsafe by a header field its reader does not see); verdict 136 is kept (no line silently means unsafe); verdict 137 is untouched (results are outside the limit; C has no code to read); verdicts 31, 118, 119, 121 and 165 are kept as the method-4 impact report says. Delegated rulings: ODR-073's reason is applied to a pointer in a field, an element or a callback result and its slot rule is kept word for word; ODR-074 and ODR-075 are kept (`ref_to_ptr` stays safe: making a raw pointer is safe, handing one to C under an assertion of safety is not). ODR-199 (the lead's, "makes a `std::function` an owned callable value") keeps its substance, but the value's default type becomes `unsafe fn(A…) -> R`, with `safe` on the entry giving `fn(A…) -> R`: a change of a delegated ruling's shape, not of an owner verdict, and it is the method-4 team's decision 4, option (a), which that team left for the owner; the owner may instead keep `fn(A…) -> R` as the default, in which case the limit refuses such an entry with no callable line to write (their option c) unless a new spelling is added.
designs.trade_offs: Safety: the only route by which safe code handed C a null, dangling, short or forged address under an assertion of safety is closed at compile time, for every carrier (field, element, union member, type argument, C++ object, callback or function-pointer result) and every spelling; C's view of memory comes from a span the compiler checked. Speed: nothing runs; the wrapper is the same single call C makes. Readability: the ordinary program's line gets shorter (`clear(ref mut frame)` instead of building a struct); the price falls on binding authors, who write `@safety` above `unsafe fn` and one `extend` wrapper per C function whose structs hold pointers, heaviest for Vulkan, where every create-info has `pNext` (the price Rust binding authors pay too); a hand binding also keeps its raw C ABI form for the unsafe declaration (ODR-074). A `std::function` entry whose parameters are plain data needs one word, `safe`, to stay callable from safe code; programs calling one today need that word or `unsafe:`. Consistency: one rule for raw pointers in both directions, judged by where the value flows (as [FFI-21a] judges pointers given back to C), one word `safe` for every foreign callable ([FFI-56] and [FFI-17a] agree), and FFI-11 and FFI-30a stay as written. Given up: option B (today: memory corruption from safe code); option C (make writing a pointer into a struct unsafe: breaks ODR-075, costs an `unsafe:` on every such line, and still leaves `buf.len = 4096` as safe code); option D (field contracts in overlays: a whole feature, barred by [FFI-30a] and verdict 132's reading). Over-reach accepted: an entry taking a `CppVector[Slice]` or a struct whose pointer C only reads is refused too, since a dangling read pointer is as unsafe as a write; the wrapper is the same.
designs.remaining_doubt: (1) [FFI-8]'s table has no row for `void*`/`const void*`; `pNext`'s refusal assumes it maps to some raw pointer type, which any mapping of `void*` must be, but the row should be checked or added by whoever owns K-questions on FFI-8. (2) Whether the owner wants the `@ffi(std_function)` default flipped to `unsafe fn(A…) -> R` (method-4's decision 4); the alternative that keeps today's default has no compiling line for a refused entry without a new spelling such as `unsafe type`. (3) Reaching type arguments (`CppVector[Slice]`) is the general reading of "as its Ember type declares it"; it refuses entries where C++ only reads the vector's length, which is acceptable but should be stated in a test. (4) K46 (J8-14) must decide `@ffi(handle)` so that `VkDevice` and `VkBuffer` fields are handles, not `*mut VkDevice_T`; until then every Vulkan struct holding a handle is also refused by this limit, which is the correct reading of the current [FFI-8] ("A `handle` is an opaque pointer-sized `Copy` value") only once the handle entry exists. (5) A `@layout(c, union)` member: [FFI-8] says union fields "are read only in `unsafe`" but not whether they are written in safe code; the limit reaches them either way, which is the safe reading. (6) The exact E5002 wording is the lead's to word (verdict 157); the lines it gives compile under DIA-25 in every spelling.

scores.holes: (1) A struct holding a C function pointer passes its limit, which names only `*T`, `*mut T`: "covers a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`) that a call carries to foreign code". Program: `// hooks.h: typedef void (*release_fn)(void*); typedef struct { release_fn release; } Hooks; void set_hooks(Hooks h); #define NO_RELEASE ((release_fn)-1)` then `unsafe extern "C": @ffi(no_callbacks) safe fn set_hooks(h: Hooks)` and `fn main(): set_hooks(Hooks(release=NO_RELEASE))`. [FFI-6a]: "A null-pointer or pointer-cast macro (`((void*)0)`, `((HANDLE)-1)`) is a `const` of that pointer type holding the address as an integer", so `NO_RELEASE` is a safe constant of type `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` ([FFI-8]: "function pointer | `unsafe extern "C" fn(…) -> R`"); the entry is accepted and C later calls address -1 from safe code. The same for a nullable function-pointer field given `None`. (2) Its carrier list is a list of shapes ("a field, a union's field, an element of a `[T; N]`, a `Span`, a `MutSpan`, an `Option` or a `CppVector`"): `Volatile[*T]` ([FFI-8]: "`volatile T*` | `Volatile[*T]`") and a `@ffi(newtype)` of a pointer typedef ("a nominal type with the typedef's representation") are reached only by charity. (3) Its own sentence contradicts itself: it lists `CppVector` among carriers and then says "a bridge type declare[s] none, `[FFI-8]`, `[FFI-17e]`", and [FFI-17e] calls `CppVector[T]` a bridge type. (4) Its E5002 registry row drops the `[FFI-56]`-first ordering but is otherwise right; its FFI-11 `retained` row edit is the one thing the other two lack.

(1) The `retained` row of [FFI-11] still reads "the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer" while its new limit says "No assertion of the fact — … an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` (`[GRM-35]`) … covers … a raw pointer" and [GRM-35] says a plain entry "asserts the function safe to call": a plain entry `fn keep(p: retained)` is refused by the limit and accepted by the row, two rules on one program (its 'why' claims the trigger spares it, but the limit's words do not). (2) A `@ffi(newtype)` of a pointer typedef is not reached by "its fields, its elements and its type arguments" (it has none); only the implementer step 1 says a newtype of a scalar is a miss, implying the pointer case is a hit, which the rule text never says. (3) [TCB-4] is not edited although [TCB-3] says "Every assumption a guarantee relies on appears in the report" and [TCB-4] lists the spellings by section; the E3100 registry row gets no `[FFI-17a]` though the row's own text is added to FFI-17a. (4) Its `safe` list for `std_function` ("a scalar, a `@layout(c)` value type or a bridge type") refuses `std::function<void(std::span<uint8_t>)>`, though [FFI-17a] maps `std::span<T>` to `MutSpan[T]`, a checked view; conservative, not unsafe. No accepted program found that breaks a promise.

(1) The same hook-table program as design 1's hole (1) is accepted: its limit reads "a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`, `ObjectPtr[C]`)" and says "a function value is not a raw pointer; what it returns is read", so a struct field of type `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)` filled from a pointer-cast constant ([FFI-6a]) or given `None` reaches C under a safe entry, and C calls it. (2) The `retained` row of [FFI-11] is left as "the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer" against its own "Every spelling that asserts the fact — `safe fn`, an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` …": the plain entry is refused by one rule and left unsafe by the other. (3) Its FFI-56 sentence "A `std::function` value is unsafe to call for the same reason, and `safe` beside `std_function` on its entry asserts it so" restates FFI-17a's rule in a second place (one rule should hold it; a cite is enough). (4) Its registry row names the spellings but not the C function pointer, consistent with its narrower limit. Otherwise sound; its doubt about `void*` having no row in [FFI-8] is real (`pNext` is `const void*`) and is K46's or a table question, not this one's.

final_edits.new:
stays unsafe to call. The diagnostic,
  `E5002`, names each missing fact and the overlay line that supplies it (`[DIA-18]`). **The limit on
  raw pointers.** No assertion of the fact — `safe fn` (`[FFI-10]`), an overlay function entry not
  written `unsafe fn` (`[GRM-35]`), or `safe` on a function-pointer typedef's or a `std_function`
  type's entry (`[FFI-56]`, `[FFI-17a]`) — covers a value the caller supplies that names memory or
  code nothing checks: a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`, an `ObjectPtr[C]`, `[FFI-23]`) or a C function
  pointer (`unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`, `[FFI-56]`) that a call carries to foreign code: as an argument
  itself; held, at any depth, by what an argument passes by value or behind a contracted pointer
  (`one`, `count(n)`, `fixed(N)`, `exclusive`, `owns`, `nullable`), read from the argument's Ember type
  as it is declared, through its fields, its elements, its type arguments (`Option`, `[T; N]`, `Span`,
  `MutSpan`, `CppVector`, `Volatile`) and the representation of a `@ffi(newtype)` (`[FFI-8]`), a C++
  method's object included; or returned, itself or inside its result, by an Ember function the call
  gives foreign code, as an argument or held by one (of a callable type only the result is read: its
  parameters are what foreign code hands the function). A type that declares no field — an `extern
  type`, an opaque class, a `@ffi(handle)` type (`[FFI-8]`), `CppString` — holds none; a `Span[T]`, a
  `MutSpan[T]`, a `CStrView` and a safe `extern "C" fn` made from an Ember function (`[FN-6]`) are
  checked views and code, not raw pointers. Safe code makes such a value null (`null[P]()`, `None`),
  one that outlives what it points at or counts fewer elements than a length beside it says
  (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or one holding any address (a pointer-cast
  constant, `[FFI-6a]`), and no contract word reaches it: words attach to parameters and results only
  (`[FFI-1]`, `[FFI-11]`), and no overlay touches a field (`[FFI-30a]`). So a declaration or entry in
  one of those spellings whose calls would carry one is `E5002` where it is written, naming the path
  to the value (`buf.data`, `pCreateInfo.pNext`, `hooks.release`, `get_buf`'s result) and the calls
  the program has: "`clear_pixels` is declared `safe fn`, but `buf.data` is a raw pointer (`*mut u8`)
  that its call hands C, and safe code can put any address in it; write `@safety("…")` above
  `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, saying what `buf.data` must point to, and put each call of
  it (line 12) in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note, or give safe callers a wrapper that fills
  `PixelBuf` from a `MutSpan[u8]` inside `unsafe:`". The lines that leave the calls unsafe are
  `@safety("…")` above the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` (a hand declaration with its C ABI
  parameters, `[FFI-10]`, ODR-074), or the typedef's or type's entry without `safe`; each call outside
  unsafe code then goes in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note (`[UNS-1]`), or behind a wrapper
  in an `extend` block (`[FFI-13]`) that fills the value from a checked view inside `unsafe:`; for an
  entry in another package's overlay, the message gives that entry as an `override` in the importing
  package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`). A message elsewhere that offers an assertion of the fact (`safe
  fn lib_step`, a `callback(…)` word, `@ffi(safe)`, `@ffi(std_function, safe)`) offers it only where
  this limit allows it (`[DIA-25]`, `[DIA-9]`). A contract with a `TODO(…)` word holds an unknown fact,
  and the first sentence of this rule decides its calls (`[FFI-11c]`). A value foreign code hands
  Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's or an export's parameter, a field of what it returns)
  is outside the limit: reading or writing through it is unsafe code (`[UNS-1]`), and `[FFI-10]`
  decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result. The check reads the declaration, the entry and the
  header's types, which every package importing the header sees alike (`[FFI-30a]`, `[BLD-16]`), and
  nothing runs for it while the program runs (§X.4, "Contract and range-type annotations").
final_edits.why: This is where the safe-to-call fact is defined and where every spelling that asserts it points, so one limit here reaches all four spellings at once and no list elsewhere can disagree. It states a property (a value the caller supplies that names memory or code nothing checks, and the direction it flows), not a shape: fields, elements, type arguments, a newtype's representation, a C++ object and a callable's result are reached alike, and types that declare no field are not. C function pointers are in the property for the same reason as data pointers: [FFI-6a] makes a pointer-cast constant of a function-pointer type a safe value, and a nullable field takes `None`, so a hook table filled by safe code is code C calls at an address nothing checks. ODR-073's reason ('a safe caller may pass a null, dangling or forged pointer') is about any assertion of safety, not about parameter slots. Naming the spellings closes the method-4 team's blocking objection (E2-1); the `TODO(…)` sentence keeps [FFI-11c] as written; the `out` sentence keeps every program that only reads what C returns.

final_edits.new: Safe code never hands foreign code an address it made up. No assertion of the fact — `safe fn` (`[FFI-10]`), an overlay function entry not written `unsafe fn` (`[GRM-35]`), `@ffi(safe)` on a function-pointer typedef (`[FFI-56]`) or `@ffi(std_function, safe)` on a `std::function` type (`[FFI-17a]`) — covers a value the caller supplies that names memory or code nothing checks: a raw pointer (`*T`, `*mut T`, an `ObjectPtr[C]`, `[FFI-54]`) or a C function pointer (`unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`, `[FFI-56]`), alone or inside an `Option`, that the call carries to foreign code: an argument itself; one held, at any depth, by what an argument passes, by value or behind a contracted pointer (`one`, `count(n)`, `fixed(N)`, `exclusive`, `owns`, `nullable`), a C++ method's object included, read from the argument's Ember type as it is declared, its fields, a union's fields, its elements and its type arguments (`[T; N]`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `Option[T]`, `CppVector[T]`); and the result, itself or at any depth in it, of a safe callable type among them (a `callback(…)` parameter's `fn(P…) -> R`, `[FFI-21]`; a field of a safe `extern "C" fn` type, which only an Ember function fills, `[FFI-56]`), since that is what an Ember function given to the call returns to foreign code, its parameters being what foreign code hands the function. A type that declares no field holds none: an `extern type`, an opaque class, a `@ffi(handle)` type (`[FFI-8]`), `CppString`; a `Span`, a `MutSpan` and a `CStrView` are checked views, not raw pointers, and only a span's elements are read. Safe code can make such a value null (`null[P]()`, `None`), pointing at fewer elements than a count beside it says or at a value already ended (`ref_to_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr()`, §IV.5, `[SPN-8]`), or holding any address (a pointer-cast constant, `[FFI-6a]`; a function pointer C handed back, whose target nothing describes), and no contract reaches it: words attach to parameters and results only (`[FFI-1]`, `[FFI-11]`), no overlay touches a field (`[FFI-30a]`), and a `safe fn`'s own function-pointer parameter, a safe `fn(P…) -> R`, takes no such value (`[FFI-21]`, `[FN-6]`). So an assertion of the fact for a function whose calls the other rules make safe, and whose calls would carry one, is `E5002` where it is written, naming where the value is held: "`clear_pixels` is declared `safe fn`, but `buf.data` is a raw pointer (`*mut u8`, line 3) that its call hands C, and safe code can put any address in it and any count in `buf.len` (line 12); write `@safety("…")` above `unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, saying what `buf.data` must point to, and put line 12 in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note, or give safe callers a wrapper that fills `PixelBuf` from a `MutSpan[u8]` inside `unsafe:`". The lines that leave the calls unsafe are `@safety("…")` above the declaration or entry written `unsafe fn` (a hand declaration keeping its C ABI parameters, `[FFI-10]`), or the typedef's or type's entry without `safe`; each call then goes in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note (`[UNS-1]`), or behind a wrapper in an `extend` block (`[FFI-13]`) that fills the value from a checked view inside `unsafe:`; for an entry in another package's overlay, the message gives that entry as an `override` in the importing package's own overlay (`[FFI-30c]`). A message elsewhere that offers an assertion of the fact (`safe fn lib_step`, a `callback(…)` word, `@ffi(safe)`) offers it only where this limit allows it (`[DIA-25]`). An entry whose own words already leave its calls unsafe (an unknown fact, a `TODO(…)` word, `retained` on a plain pointer; `[FFI-11]`, `[FFI-11c]`) is as it was. A value foreign code hands Ember (a result, an `out` value, a callback's parameter, a field of what it returns) is outside this limit: reading or writing through it is unsafe code (`[UNS-1]`), and `[FFI-10]` decides a hand declaration's raw-pointer result. The limit is read from the declaration and the header's types, which every package importing the header sees alike (`[FFI-30a]`, `[BLD-16]`), and nothing runs for it while the program runs.
