     `static mut` and runs no code the compiler cannot read whole (a call through a function value,

designs.accepted_program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Atomic, Lock

static DONE: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection, made on a scoped task's thread
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool: takes a lock, so `Conn` is not plain
        id = this.id
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object: connections to close
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

class Inbox:                                  # batches waiting for the closer thread
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    items: Array[Batch] guarded by lock = []

fn close_all(inbox: thread_shared Inbox):     # the closer thread lets the batches go
    while DONE.load() == 0:
        with inbox.lock:
            inbox.items.clear()               # ends each Batch and its Conn: the Conn's drop runs here, on this thread
    with inbox.lock:
        inbox.items.clear()

fn open_one(pool: thread_shared Pool, inbox: thread_shared Inbox):
    with inbox.lock:
        inbox.items.push(owns Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)]))

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    inbox = thread_shared Inbox()
    closer = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared inbox: close_all(inbox))
    with pool.lock:
        with s = thread.scope():
            s.spawn(owns fn(): open_one(pool, inbox))
        println(pool.free.len())              # 0: the Conn's drop, on the closer, waits for this lock
    DONE.store(1)
    closer.join()
    with pool.lock:
        println(pool.free.len())              # 1

# This is E3-1's program. It compiles: the task's summary changes `inbox.items` under `inbox.lock`, not
# `pool.free`, so the scope's end under `pool.lock` is not [THR-19]'s case; the closer's `clear()` is a
# written end of the Conn ([DRP-8]), taking a `Pool`'s lock while holding an `Inbox`'s, two kinds.
# It runs: the Conn is marked handed over at its making twice over (a task's thread; a type that is
# not plain), so nothing is queued to the task's thread, the task ends with nothing hidden to run, the
# scope ends, main prints 0 and lets the lock go, the closer's waiting drop pushes 1, and after the
# join main prints 1. Output: 0 then 1, on every run.
designs.runtime_cost: Row "A `thread_shared` value's two counts" (§X.4, [COST-3]). What runs: (1) inside the runtime's allocation of a `thread_shared` block, one load of the thread's kind (a thread-local the chunk allocation already consults) and one store of the handed-over mark into the header it is writing, for a value made on a thread other than main or a `thread.spawn` thread; (2) for a value of a type that is not plain, the making line emits the marked making the `using`-instance making already uses (no test: the fact is compiled in); (3) for every value so marked, each count operation is the existing atomic away-path operation instead of a plain add, measured as one atomic count against two: a pipeline 27% faster on one thread, a thread's own values 25% slower; (4) a check point stays one thread-local load and a branch, now also inside lock blocks, walks and scope blocks, with none moved and none added; (5) nothing per check point for placement, no per-thread hold number, no function copies, no worker wake, no step at a return to C; (6) at a hot reload that makes a type stop being plain, one store per live value of that type during the walk prepare already makes.
designs.implementer_steps: 1. Interface fact "plain" per type: in the package that declares a type, compute from the drop's effect set (EFF-1) and summary (EFF-24) and from the plain bits of every owned type (imports' interface files; thread_shared owners included; `dyn I`, function values, `open`/`abstract` owned objects are not plain; a greatest fixpoint over the package's own type graph for cycles). Write the bit beside the layout in the interface file (BLD-14 item list) and in `TypeInfo` (RT-3) for `ember inspect --cost`. 2. Making lines: when the compiler lowers `thread_shared T(...)` (and generic instances, MONO-1), if T's plain bit is clear it emits the marked-making entry point already used for `using` an instance (N84): home 0, away 1, handed-over mark set. 3. Runtime thread kind: a thread-local flag "home thread" set for main at start-up and for threads `thread.spawn` starts; left clear for job workers, for any thread the runtime starts to run a scope's tasks, and for host threads at `ember_rt_thread_attach()`. The allocation of a `thread_shared` block in `Global` reads it: clear means mark set, away 1, home 0 (the chunk record is still written, unused for marked values). A `@parallel` chunk the calling thread runs itself inherits that thread's flag by construction. 4. Check points: keep the current placement (back edges, before and after blocking calls, the thread's end, after a join or a scope's end); remove nothing, add nothing, and emit them inside lock blocks, walks and scope blocks as anywhere else. No contribution to effects or summaries. 5. Thread end: the runtime's thread-exit path drains and closes the queue (RC-4 point 3) before it signals the join handle, so `join` returns after the last queued drop. 6. Hot reload: plan compares the plain bit as a fact (HR-44); when it goes from set to clear, prepare sets the handed-over mark on each live `thread_shared` instance of that type during its list walk (HR-12). 7. Diagnostics: no new code; THR-19's join and scope-end messages unchanged. 8. Tests: E3-1's program prints `0 1`; J7-01's program (main's Conn ended by a worker) prints frames then `1`, the drop running on the worker when main's lock is free; J7-02's program prints "texture 1 freed", "texture 2 freed" during `bundles.clear()` on main; a scoped job that makes a Texture whose drop writes main's `static mut LOG` and that main clears after the join writes LOG on main only (no race); a `thread.spawn` thread's own plain values keep the plain-add path (the 25% row); an `ember inspect --cost` run names the row for a marked making.
designs.departs_from_verdict: None. Verdict 101 (two numbers; the making thread deletes at its next check point, always before the thread ends; fix 2 moves A into B at a hand-over the compiler sees) is kept: the two counts stay for every value made on main or a spawned thread with a plain type, the queue and check points stay, and the two new marks are fix 2's step taken at the making line, as the lead's N84 already took it for a value made `using` an instance; the owner should see that the set of values counted atomically from the start is wider than N84's (touches 101, within fix 2). Verdict 43 kept: nothing is checked while running and no hidden end can wait for a lock its thread holds, because a drop that takes a lock never waits in a queue. Verdict 57 kept: every end with outside effects runs as a written call where the last owner ends, so BRW-18, RC-5 and the summaries see it; the only end no line writes changes nothing outside its object. Verdict 104 kept: a task's claims end at its join, and nothing runs on its behalf after it. Verdict 114 kept: a one-thread object is never queued. Verdicts 86 and 88 untouched (no copies are needed). The method-4 team's decision 4, left for the owner (a value queued to a host thread gone back to C), is decided here by the by-thread mark, its option c narrowed to host-thread-made values, with no per-call step; the owner may still prefer their option b. The method-4 team's decisions 1 (placement by judgement), 2 (worker wake) and 3 (atomic from the making line only for drops reaching main's statics in jobs) are superseded by the same two sentences, which the arbiter's E3-1 showed those decisions could not close together.
designs.trade_offs: Given up: the plain-add speed of the two-count design for two sets of values. (i) Values of types whose drop does anything but free memory and end what it owns (logs, takes a lock, writes an atomic, calls C with callbacks, reaches a `static mut`): every count operation on them is atomic, the cost the owner measured as 9% to 13% for a random mix against two counts; such a drop already pays a lock or a syscall, and the owner's measured gains (a thread's own values, the camera program) are on plain data. (ii) Values made in scoped tasks, jobs, worker-run chunks and C callbacks: atomic from the start; for the usual shape (made on a worker, consumed elsewhere) the measured pipeline row says this is 27% faster than two counts on one thread and equal on more, and only a task that makes and ends its own `thread_shared` values locally loses the 25%, a shape `owns` serves without any count. Against the four goals: speed, nothing new runs at check points and nothing is added to a hot loop (one load and one store move into an allocation that already writes the header); readability, nothing to write and nothing refused that compiles today, `join` means done, a queued drop's output may appear later only for a value whose drop prints nothing (it is plain); safety, no hidden end can ever run where its written call would be refused (lock, walk, view, task, contract) or after the window THR-11 checked (the post-join race of a worker-run drop on main's `static mut` is gone), and no value waits for a thread that sleeps in the pool or in C; consistency, THR-20's headline becomes true, THR-11's 'a task touches no one-thread count' becomes complete, verdict 43's promise holds with no list of rules, and the compiler needs no per-place judgement, copies or per-thread number, so BLD-16 is met by construction (the plain bit is a declaring-package fact in the interface file; the thread's kind is run-time data read where the block is laid out). Compared with the method-4 design: fewer mechanisms (no placement analysis, no wake, no return-to-C point), one honest cost row instead of three, and one closed contradiction instead of an open one.
designs.remaining_doubt: (1) A `thread.spawn` thread blocked for its life in one call (a hand-written worker in `rx.recv()`) runs its check point before and after the call, so a plain value queued to it while it blocks is freed only when the call returns or the thread ends: memory held, never a hang or a resource (a resource-holding drop is not plain and never queues). The owner may want the text to name this bound in point 5 or to pay a wake (one futex per first queued value) as the method-4 team proposed for pool workers; this ruling does not. (2) The 25% and 27% figures are the owner's measurements of other shapes; the cost of atomics on task-made values should be measured once (the pipeline row is the nearest evidence). (3) Plainness excludes `Io`, so a drop that writes a log file counts atomically; the alternative, allowing `Io`, would need check points kept out of `@noio` functions transitively, which a separately compiled callee cannot know (BLD-16), so the stricter set was chosen. (4) The by-thread mark assumes the runtime starts every scope task's thread or runs it on a worker it owns; if an implementation ran a scope's task on a thread the program made with `thread.spawn`, the flag of that thread would have to be cleared for the task's duration; THR-5 and §XI.5 do not say where a `thread.scope()` task runs, and the lead may wish to pin it. (5) The wording 'a check point is not a line or a call for the rules that judge where it stands' relies on the argument that what the queue ends has no owner left so no view, walk or task reads it; a `weakref thread_shared T` name holds a count (RC-5 point 2), so its target is never at zero; I found no view that escapes this, but it is the one claim an attacker should try again.

designs.question: K10: Where and when does a queued `thread_shared` value's `drop` run, and how is a wait inside a held lock in a `with scope` block kept from hanging when a task makes a value another thread lets go of? (Angle: the newcomer's one-sentence rule first, then safety and cost.)
designs.summary: The newcomer's rule: a `thread_shared` value made by `main` or by a `thread.spawn` thread goes home to be ended, at that thread's next check point where it holds no lock; a value made anywhere else (a scoped task's thread, a job worker, a `@parallel` chunk, a thread C owns) is counted with atomics from its making line and is ended wherever its last owner is let go. For the threads that keep a home count, a check point empties the queue only while the thread holds no lock, kept by a plain per-thread count of held locks whose release to zero is itself a check point (J7-01), a check point is added where a callback returns to C and none stands inside a function carrying a contract; a `thread.spawn` thread's function counts the `drop`s of the `thread_shared` values made on it, so a `join` of it inside a lock those `drop`s take is `E7018` when compiling, as verdict 43 and `[THR-19]` promise.

designs.accepted_program:
```ember
import std.thread                              # the arbiter's E3-1 program, unchanged
from std.sync import Atomic, Lock

static DONE: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

class Pool:                                    # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                    # one connection, made on a scoped task's thread
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                 # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                   # a plain object: connections to close
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

class Inbox:                                   # batches waiting for the closer thread
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    items: Array[Batch] guarded by lock = []

fn close_all(inbox: thread_shared Inbox):      # the closer thread: lets the batches go
    while DONE.load() == 0:
        with inbox.lock:
            inbox.items.clear()                # ends each Batch and its Conn
    with inbox.lock:
        inbox.items.clear()

fn open_one(pool: thread_shared Pool, inbox: thread_shared Inbox):
    with inbox.lock:
        inbox.items.push(owns Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)]))

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    inbox = thread_shared Inbox()
    closer = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared inbox: close_all(inbox))
    with pool.lock:
        with s = thread.scope():
            s.spawn(owns fn(): open_one(pool, inbox))
        println(pool.free.len())
    DONE.store(1)
    closer.join()
    with pool.lock:
        println(pool.free.len())
```

Compiles: the task's function pushes to `inbox.items` under `inbox.lock` and ends no `Conn`, so it changes nothing `pool.lock` guards, and a scoped task's thread owes no `drop` (`[THR-11]`, `[RC-4]` point 1), so the scope's end inside `with pool.lock:` is not `E7018`. Runs: the `Conn` is made on the task's thread, so it is marked handed over at its making and counted in its away count; the closer's `clear` takes that count to zero and ends the `Conn` there, whose `drop` waits for `pool.lock` until `main`'s block ends (`main` waits for nothing the closer does inside that block). Prints `0` (the free list is empty while `main` holds the lock), then `1` (the closer's last `clear`, and so the `drop`, finish before `closer.join()` returns). The same every run. J7-02's program compiles too and prints `texture 1 freed`, `texture 2 freed` during `bundles.clear()` on `main`, then the frames. J7-01's program compiles; the `Conn`'s `drop` runs where `main`'s `with pool.lock:` block ends, later frames print `1`, and `h.join()` prints `1`.
designs.runtime_cost: Row "A lock": one plain add of the thread's held-lock count at each lock taking and one plain subtract at each release, with one thread-local load and branch (the queue test) when the count reaches zero. Row "A `thread_shared` value's two counts": the check point stays one thread-local load and one branch; the queue's work (out of line) now runs only while the thread holds no lock; one queue test at each callback's return to C; atomic count operations from the making line for every `thread_shared` value made on a scoped task's thread, a job worker, a `@parallel` chunk or a thread C owns (the measured 25% of a thread's own values is lost for a task's own shared values; the pipeline shape, made on one thread and ended on the next, measured 27% slower under two counts on one thread, gains). Rows "An Ember function called by C through a function pointer" and "An export's or a trampoline's entry": one queue test at the return. Nothing new at any written line, at any check point's hot path, at a scope's end or at a thread's end.
designs.implementer_steps:
1. Runtime, thread registration (`[HR-3a]`): each registered thread records whether it has a home count: the main thread and `thread.spawn` threads yes; scoped task threads (however the runtime runs them, own threads or pool workers), job workers and host threads attached by `ember_rt_thread_attach` no. Only a thread with a home count has a queue.
2. Runtime, allocation (`[OBJ-1]`): a chunk taken by a thread without a home count gets the no-thread id in its header; a `thread_shared` block from such a chunk is initialised with the handed-over mark set in its away word, exactly as a block made `using` an instance is, and its first owner goes to the away count. No change to the inlined count operations of `[RT-10]`: the id compare fails for every thread, the mark test takes the away path.
3. Runtime, locks: a thread-local `locks_held`; `ember_rt_lock_take` adds one, `ember_rt_lock_release` subtracts one and, when zero and the queue head is not null, calls the out-of-line drain (`ember_rt_checkpoint`). The drain itself returns at once when `locks_held` is not zero, so every existing check point keeps its one load and branch. The compiler may omit a check point it can prove lies under a lock in the same function; not observable.
4. Compiler, check points (`[RC-4]` point 3): as today at back edges, before and after blocking calls (a `join`, a scope's end, a receive, a sleep, a lock wait) and at the thread's end before the join is signalled; add one after the body in every export and trampoline wrapper (beside `[FFI-22]`'s attach test); emit none inside a function carrying a contract of §X.2, nor in its C wrapper. The scope's end waits for its tasks only (`[THR-5]`); tasks have no queue to drain.
5. Compiler, summaries (`[EFF-24]`): record the set of `thread_shared` types a function may make (its own lines plus callees, function values by `[EFF-2]`), written to the interface file like "what it may end". `[THR-20]`: the function given to `thread.spawn` counts the `drop` of each made type as possibly run on that thread (for `E7012` and for the lock kinds it may take); `[THR-19]`'s join clause reads it, so `h.join()` under a lock of a kind one of those `drop`s takes is `E7018`, with the message above.
6. Tests (break-tested): the accepted program prints `0` then `1` under a stress loop; the refused program is `E7018` at line 40 and compiles with the join moved; J7-02's program prints the two `freed` lines during the clear; J7-01's program prints `1` at the join; a program that holds a lock while a worker lets a main-made value go, with a loop back edge inside the lock, runs the drop exactly when the block ends (a counter of drop runs read under the lock inside the block is 0, after it 1); a contract function with a back edge drains nothing inside it (an `@noblock` spin loop with a queued value, the drop runs after the function returns).
7. Separate compilation and modules (`[BLD-16]`, `[ABI-1]`): every package emits the same lock-count operations and check-point tests; no package needs to know which `thread_shared` types exist or which threads make them; the made-type set travels in interface files as other summary facts do. Hot reload (Annex B): the queue, the held-lock count and the home-count flag are runtime thread state, not image state (`[HR-4a]`); a commit runs only with every thread's `[HR-42]` depth at zero, so never inside a drain. FFI: a host thread has no queue, so a value made in a callback on a C-owned thread is ended wherever its last owner ends; the main thread driven by a C event loop drains at each callback's return.
designs.departs_from_verdict: Verdict 101 in its letter, for the owner (ODR): "The thread that made the object counts its owners in one number, A" no longer holds for a scoped task's thread, a job worker or a thread C owns, whose values count in B from the making line. The substance is kept: two numbers for the main thread and every `thread.spawn` thread, the queue, check points placed by the compiler, deletion always before the thread ends (a spawn thread's end empties its queue before its join returns; nothing is ever queued to a thread joined as a task), the ended-thread path word for word; counting away from the making line is fix 2's step at the making line, which N84 (decisions.md section 13) already took for a value made `using` an instance and reported as touching verdict 101. Verdict 43 kept in full: no written line is checked while running; the held-lock count decides only when hidden code runs and refuses nothing. Verdicts 56, 57 (ends still count as calls at the ender; `[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-24]` unchanged), 104, 114 untouched. Verdict 166 (a scoped task neither makes nor ends a `shares` owner, a count with no atomics) is followed into the home count.
designs.trade_offs: Speed: a `thread_shared` value made inside a scoped task, a job or a `@parallel` chunk pays atomic count operations (verdict 101's measurement: a thread's own values 25% faster under two counts, lost for a task's own shared values), while the common shape, a value a task makes for its parent to end, gains (the pipeline row: two counts 27% slower on one thread); the lock count costs two plain instructions per lock, beside C's lock; the check point's hot path and every written line are unchanged. The alternative kept for the lead, design B: a scoped task's thread keeps a home count and at its end hands its queue, closed, to the parent, which drains it at its next check point outside every lock; it keeps the two-count speed for task-internal sharing at the price of a splice at each task's end, a parent that reads another thread's final home counts, a rule that a value already queued is ended only by the queue's taker (else a subtract that finds the queue closed and the parent would both end it), and nothing for job workers and C threads, which would still need the atomic rule or a wake of idle workers; it composes with everything else here. Readability: no word to write, no new refusal but the join under a lock whose fix moves one line (verdict 43's own shape); a newcomer holds one sentence: made by main or a spawned thread, ended at home when free of locks; made anywhere else, ended where let go. Safety: all atomic for the no-home-count values; for the others the drain runs only on the making thread (the sole writer of the home count), and the held-lock count keeps a queued drop out of the lock it takes; walks and views need no keep-out because every other place a queued drop could change is guarded, atomic, or a module variable whose change by a value another thread may end is already `E7012`/`E7007`. Consistency: `[THR-11]`'s "a task touches no one-thread count" becomes literally true of the home count; `[THR-20]`'s headline becomes true for queued values; `[THR-19]`'s and verdict 43's promise holds for `join` and for a scope's end. Given up: a thread that holds a lock, or sits in a contract function, for its whole life defers the drops queued to it until it releases, returns or ends (as any thread needing that lock would wait); a C-driven main thread drains at callback returns, not inside C.
designs.remaining_doubt: (1) Whether the owner accepts narrowing verdict 101's A to threads the program owns; the lead may instead take design B for `thread.scope` tasks and the atomic rule for workers and C threads only. (2) `[RC-4]` point 4's "travelled inside another object": `[THR-2]` already walks a stored object's contents at a store under a lock and stops at a `thread_shared` value; letting that walk also hand over each `thread_shared` owner it meets when the storing thread is the maker would shrink the queue to objects stored by non-makers, within fix 2; not changed here, since verdict 101 accepted the delay for that shape. (3) The old text quoted in the edits is copied with CURRENT-SPEC.md's line wrapping; the lead's asserting script may need the unwrapped form. (4) The `E7018` message's wording for the join should be checked against the DIA rules. (5) A `Once` initialiser (`[STA-3]`) running at a check point whose queued drop reads the same static would recurse into the once-flag, exactly as a written call there would; the current text does not treat it either. (6) The atomic cost for task-internal shared values is inferred from verdict 101's rows, not measured for this shape; measure on the laptop's performance cores before the hardening is cut.

scores.holes: (1) A pool worker's queue is not partitioned by job. Design 1's point 3 drains 'at the end of every task, job and `@parallel` chunk a thread runs, before its end is let go to what waits for it'. `[JOB-2]`: '`jobs.scope()` follows `[THR-5]` and `[THR-11]`', and §XI.5: 'The job system is a pool of worker threads'. So a `jobs.scope()` job's end drains the worker's whole queue, which may hold a value an earlier job of another scope made on that worker (point 2 queues to 'the making thread'). Program: job A (scope 1, earlier) makes `thread_shared Conn(pool=...)` inside a plain `Batch` pushed to an inbox; later `with pool.lock:` / `with s = jobs.scope(): s.submit(owns fn(): sum(xs))`; a closer thread clears the inbox during the second scope; the Conn is queued to the worker; the worker running `sum` reaches its job's last check point (hold zero) and runs `Conn.drop`, which waits for `pool.lock` held by main at the scope's end: hang. The job's function is charged only with 'the `drop` of every `thread_shared` value made on its thread, by its body or a function it runs' (design 1's THR-11 text); `sum` makes none, so nothing is refused, and verdict 43's 'nothing is checked while running' is broken by a hang. The design's remaining doubt (1) admits the thread model is unpinned; the text does not hold 'either way'. (2) The hold count is a run-time branch inside every lock block that may reach a check point, a cost the owner may read as a check (the design's doubt 2), and the 'may travel' over-approximation refuses scope ends and joins that cannot hang (doubt 3). (3) `E7007` for a parent that reads an unguarded `static mut` a task-made value's `drop` changes refuses programs the current text and verdict 104 accept, since the drop's time (the task's last point) is invented by the design. (4) Readability: six mechanisms (hold count, loop-kind placement, wake, dead-value hand to main, made-type charge, contract hand-over) for one question.

(1) The plainness definition contradicts itself as written: §X.1's row '`Sync` | an atomic read-modify-write stronger than relaxed, a lock, a channel operation, thread spawn or join, making or ending a `thread_shared` owner or a `weakref thread_shared T` link'. A type that owns a `thread_shared` child ends that owner in its `drop`, so its effect set has `Sync`, and the design's 'has none of the effects a contract may forbid (... `Sync` ...)' makes every such type non-plain while the same sentence says 'every type the value owns is plain, all the way down, `thread_shared` owners included'. Fixed in the merged edit: the `Sync` of ending the `thread_shared` owners the value holds is excepted (that end is the runtime's step wherever the value ends). (2) Hot reload: the design's `[HR-44]` edit marks live values handed over when a type stops being plain, but a value already in a home thread's queue (queued mark set, counts at zero) is then ended by that thread's next check point, which may stand inside a lock the new `drop` takes. `[HR-12]`: 'Plan and prepare walk the list only while every other registered thread is at depth zero', and a thread blocked in a lock wait is at depth zero while holding another lock. Fixed in the merged edit: plan refuses such a reload (`E9030`) while a value of the type is queued. (3) The thread model is unpinned (doubt 4): if a scope's task could run on the thread that opened the scope, the by-thread mark would be missed. Fixed by pinning it in point 4. (4) A plain value queued to a `thread.spawn` thread blocked for its life in `rx.recv()` holds memory until the call returns or the thread ends; no resource and no hang, named in point 5. Nothing else broke: a plain `drop` frees memory and ends what it owns, so no lock (`[THR-19]`), walk (`[BRW-18]`), view (`[RC-5]`: what the queue ends has no owner and no opened `weakref thread_shared T` name, which 'holds one count for its life'), contract (§X.2) or task window (`[THR-11]`) can see it.

(1) Walks and views have no keep-out, on the claim that a module variable changed by a queued drop 'is already `E7012` (`[THR-20]`) or `E7007` (`[THR-11]`)'. False for a scoped task that lets go of a value the main thread made. Program: `static mut LOG: Array[String] = []`; `class Conn: fn drop(): LOG.push(owns String("closed"))`; in `main`: `b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn()])`; `with s = thread.scope(): s.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())` (the task ends the Conn's last owner: point 2 queues it to main, since `[THR-11]`'s window ends at the join and the task touched `LOG` at no moment the parent used it); then `for line in LOG: helper()`. Design 3 keeps 'every loop's back edge' as a check point, main holds no lock, so the drain runs `Conn.drop` inside the walk and pushes to `LOG`, which `[BRW-18]` promises 'nothing changes ... whatever the change': the walked array may reallocate under its view, a use after free. `E7012` needs 'a function that may run on another thread' from `[THR-20]`'s list, which excludes scoped tasks; `E7007` needs a conflict inside the scope, and there is none. (2) Contracts: 'none stands in the lines of a function that carries a contract' leaves the check points of its callees: a `@noblock` function calling a looping callee drains a `Block`ing drop inside its promise (`[EFF-5]`, `E4003` promised when compiling, broken while running). (3) Design B (hand the queue to the parent) is offered to the lead without text, and the lock count is a run-time branch at every lock release (one load and a test), the kind of check verdict 43 may not accept. (4) The by-thread mark itself is right and is the part the merged ruling keeps.

judgements.grafts: From design 3: the `[WK-3]` cross-reference edit (design 2 left `[WK-3]` claiming 'is ended at its making thread's next check point' for every value) and the `[OBJ-1]` sentence that says no thread asks which thread made a value marked at its making (so the chunk record is unused for it); its one-sentence newcomer rule is used as the shape of `[RC-4]` point 5. From design 1: 'before its end is let go to what waits for it' as the words for a thread's last check point (design 2 wrote 'before its `join` returns', which does not name a scope's end), and the statement that the queue's own atomic step and the ends of what the value owns are the runtime's, counted in no function's effect set. Taken from neither, added by the judge: the `Sync` exception in the plainness definition (hole 1 of design 2); the `E9030` refusal while a value of a type that stops being plain is queued (hole 2); the pin that a scope's task or job runs on a thread the runtime owns, never on the thread that opened the scope (hole 3 of design 2, doubt 1 of design 1). Rejected from design 1: the hold count, loop-kind placement, worker wake, dead-value hand to main, made-type charge (`[EFF-24]`) and the `E7007`/`E7018` refusals of task-made drops, all unnecessary once nothing a task makes is queued and only a plain drop waits. Rejected from design 3: the held-lock count and the contract exclusion, both run-time or incomplete, and design B.

judgements.remaining_doubt: (1) The pin that a scope's task or job runs on a thread the runtime owns, never on the thread that opened the scope, is written into `[RC-4]` point 4 here; `[THR-5]` and §XI.5 do not say it, so the lead should check the runtime's design (M9) and, if a scope's task may run on the opening thread, have the runtime clear that thread's home flag for the task's duration instead. (2) The `Sync` exception in plainness lets a plain `drop`'s atomic subtracts of its `thread_shared` children, and the queue's own compare-exchange, run inside a `@nosync` function at a check point; the current text already runs the queue's step there, and `@nosync` forbids the function's own effect set, not the runtime's steps, but the owner may want the word 'runtime's steps' said once in §X.2. (3) Plainness excludes `Io`, so a `drop` that writes a log counts atomically; allowing `Io` would need check points kept out of `@noio` functions transitively, which a separately compiled callee cannot know (`[BLD-16]`), so the stricter set was chosen; the cost is on types that already pay a syscall. (4) The 25% and 27% figures are the owner's measurements of other shapes; the atomic cost on task-made and non-plain values should be measured once on the performance cores before the hardening is cut. (5) A plain value queued to a `thread.spawn` thread blocked for its life in one call holds memory until the call returns or the thread ends; point 5 names it; a wake (one futex per first queued value) would remove it at a cost the owner may or may not want. (6) The refused program of the ruling is refused by the current text already (`[THR-19]`'s join clause with `[THR-20]`); the ruling adds no refusal, and the lead's test set should carry the arbiter's E3-1 program as a run-pass test printing `0` then `1`, J7-01's as frames then `1`, J7-02's as two `freed` lines during the clear, and a break test that removes the by-thread mark (E3-1's program then hangs or races) and one that removes the by-type mark (J7-01's program then hangs at the inner walk). scores.holes: No accepted program found that breaks a promise: the hold count is dynamic (a callee's back edge inside a contract function's extent sees hold > 0), a walk or view rooted in a `static mut` holds it across a generator's pause, and a worker's drop reaching an unguarded `static mut` is handed to main. The holes are over-refusal and weight. (1) It refuses programs that cannot hang: its THR-11 text counts "the `drop` of every such value, from its making line to the task's end" and its summary says "when unsure, it may travel", so a scoped task that makes `thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)` into a `Batch` it pushes onto the parent's own list `made` (a real variable, no third thread), while the parent holds `with pool.lock:` around the scope, is `E7018` at the scope's end, though nothing ends the `Conn` during the task and the current text's THR-19 clause ("the end of a `with scope` block, whose task changes what the held lock guards") was meant for a change the task's lines make. Likewise its E7007 extension ("what those `drop`s change is the task's own change, checked ... against the parent") refuses a parent that reads an unguarded `static mut` the `Conn`'s `drop` writes during the scope, a race that needs a third thread the program has not got. (2) The THR-19 edit keeps "changes what the held lock guards" while its message reads by kind ("takes a `Pool`'s lock (line 14)"); the two readings differ for `this.pool.lock` against main's `pool.lock`, and the text does not say which. (3) Seven mechanisms (hold count with four kinds of place, back-edge placement rule, worker wake, dead hand to main, contract-based point-4 mark, made-type summary, last-point counting) for one question; the owner's condition is the elegant shape, and a newcomer cannot hold this in a sentence. (4) Its remaining doubt (1) is real: whether a scope's task runs on its own thread or a worker changes which thread runs a `drop` queued after the join, and the text is written to hold either way at the cost of the dead-hand path.

No accepted program found that breaks a promise: every `drop` with an outside effect runs where its last owner ends, as a written call the existing rules judge (`[DRP-8]`: "Anything that may end a value whose type has a `drop` ... makes the changes that `drop` makes, wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them"); what the queue ends frees memory only. The holes are in the letter. (1) Cost, not safety: the effect table says `Sync` is "making or ending a `thread_shared` owner or a `weakref thread_shared T` link", so by the design's own words ("its `drop`'s effect set (`[EFF-1]`) has none of the effects a contract may forbid (§X.2: `Alloc`, `Sync`, ...)") a `Conn` with `pool: thread_shared Pool` and no `drop` at all is not plain, and every object graph of `thread_shared` objects pays atomics; the count steps of ending what the value holds must be carved out (grafted below). (2) Hot reload: its HR-44 edit "sets the handed-over mark on every live `thread_shared` value of the type ... one store each" loses the home count: point 4's hand-over "first adds its own count of the value into the away count and marks the value handed over"; and a value already queued (queued mark set) when the type stops being plain would have its new, non-plain `drop` run at the home thread's next check point, where no rule judged it (fixed below). (3) `[WK-3]`'s last sentence ("is ended at its making thread's next check point (`[RC-4]` point 5), and its `drop` runs there") is left unqualified, true but no longer the whole story (fixed below). (4) A `@nosync` function's check point still performs the queue's acquire and compare-exchange when a value is queued, `Sync` by the table's letter; the design calls a check point "not a line or a call" for §X.2, which is the right reading (the handed-over test before a count operation is likewise the runtime's), but the owner may want it said. (5) E3-1's program with a stream of batches (an `open_some` loop in the task) can still deadlock: the closer runs `Conn`'s `drop` under `inbox.lock` and waits for `pool.lock`, the task waits for `inbox.lock`, main holds `pool.lock` waiting for the task; this is a lock-order cycle across three threads, written in the source (`Conn.drop` takes `pool.lock`, called by `inbox.items.clear()`), which `[THR-19]` never promised to refuse ("A wait for a lock this thread holds"), so it is no promise broken, but the lead should know the design closes the hidden hang, not every hang.

Two accepted programs break promises, both from "Walks and views need no keep-out: besides its own object a queued drop can change only guarded places (the lock count), atomics, and module variables, and a module variable changed by the drop of a value another thread may end is already `E7012` (`[THR-20]`) or `E7007` (`[THR-11]`, through `[DRP-8]`)" and from "none stands in the lines of a function that carries a contract". (1) `static mut LOG: Array[String] = []`; `class Conn: fn drop(): LOG.push(owns String("closed"))`; `gen fn lines(): for l in LOG: yield l`; in `main`: `b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn()])` (made on main), `with pool.lock:`, inside it `with s = thread.scope(): s.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())` (the task ends `b`, so the `Conn` is queued to main), then still inside the lock block `g = lines()`, `first = g.next()`; after the block `println(g.next())`. `[THR-11]` accepts it (the parent reads `LOG` only after the join, verdict 104; the task was not started inside a walk), `[THR-20]` accepts it (a scoped task may reach a `static mut`). Under this design the check point after the scope's end does not drain ("only while the thread holds no lock"), the release of `pool.lock` is a check point and runs `Conn`'s `drop`, which pushes to `LOG` while `g` is paused in a walk of `LOG`: `[BRW-18]` ("or a generator that walks it ... will still be used, nothing changes the collection") is broken, and a reallocation of `LOG` under the generator's element view is a use after free. (2) `@noblock fn spin(): while not READY.load(): step()` with `fn step():` a plain function containing a loop: the design keeps check points out of `spin`'s own lines only, so `step`'s back edge drains main's queue inside `spin`'s run and a queued `Conn`'s `drop` takes `pool.lock`, a `Block` inside a `@noblock` function; `[EFF-5]` ("Each contract in the table forbids its effect in the function's effect set") is broken by code no effect set holds. Design 1's dynamic hold and design 2's plain-type rule both close these; design 3's static rule does not. Also, its EFF-24 "made types" summary and THR-20 count exist only to make `h.join()` under a lock `E7018`, which under design 2 needs nothing (a plain `drop` takes no lock).

judgements.grafts: From design 3 (index 2): (a) the `[OBJ-1]` sentence that a chunk of a thread without a home count names no thread and its blocks are laid out marked handed over, which is how \"marked at its making\" costs nothing at the making line beyond the header the allocation writes anyway; (b) the check point where an exported function or trampoline returns to C, with its two §X.4 rows, so a main thread driven by a C event loop frees plain values queued to it between callbacks (design 2's queue holds memory only, but a loop-free callback program would hold it until exit); (c) its honesty about verdict 101: the ruling narrows which threads keep the home count A, and is reported as touching 101, as N84 was. From design 1 (index 0): (d) no check point at the back edge of a loop of plain operations (one whose body makes no call and no operation on an `Atomic` or a channel end): the per-iteration thread-local load and branch leaves every leaf loop, which keeps C's code and vectorisation where it matters, and is safe under design 2 because a plain end owes nothing but memory and a finite leaf loop reaches its end, the next point; (e) `jobs.wait` named among the blocking calls. Not taken: design 1's hold count, worker wake, dead hand to main and task-function counting (none is needed once nothing queued has an outside effect and nothing is queued to a task's thread); design 3's lock count, made-type summary and `[THR-19]`/`[THR-20]` join clauses (a plain `drop` takes no lock, so a join under a lock cannot hang through the queue and the existing join clause suffices). The task's two suggested alternatives, weighed and not taken: \"a scoped task's thread is the parent's for counting\" degenerates to the by-thread mark: the task's own count steps cannot be plain adds on the parent's home count (the parent may write it at the same moment, `[THR-11]` \"A task touches no one-thread count\"), so they must go to the away count, and a value made with home 0 must be marked handed over at birth or an away subtract reaching zero ends nobody; that is design 2's rule with the chunk in the parent's pool and no gain. \"A check point at the join that the lock holder runs\" (the task hands its queue to the parent) runs a lock-taking `drop` on a thread holding that lock unless deferred to the lock's release, which needs a hold count and a third thread running the `drop`, and refuses nothing a reader could see; rejected. rulings.title: How do C++ overloaded functions and constructors import into Ember?

designs.question: K21 (J8-04): How do C++ overloaded functions and constructors import into Ember? How is an overload set named, how is an ambiguous use refused, how does an overlay entry (and `rename`/`hide`) name one overload, what does `ember bind` write, and which codes; with default arguments, `super.init` ([FFI-39b]) and overrides covered, nothing running while the program runs, and nothing of the whole program read by a package ([BLD-16]).
designs.summary: A C++ name the header declares for several functions (functions, methods, static functions, constructors as `new`, the listed instances of a function template, a function with default arguments once per count of arguments it accepts) is one Ember name, exempt from [TYP-26] because the program declared none of them; each use stands for one function, chosen when compiling from the use's own words in three steps that reuse [TYP-24]'s ranking (count and names; exact types, a literal as its default type, the receiver as its name's kind; then [TYP-5]'s coercions, a literal as a type of its own kind, a changeable name reaching a reading method as a view), and none or several is the new `E5035`, naming each function and the line to write. An overlay entry, a `rename` and a `hide` name one function by the name alone where it has one, otherwise by the parameters' count, names, words and types (and a result type) written in Ember's own spelling, `@ffi(const)` naming the `const` one of a pair; an entry fitting none or several is `E5010`; `ember bind --init` writes one entry per function and `ember.overlays` keeps one keyed line per function. Every function keeps its own thunk, entry, `@safety` and record line, so a call is the same direct, LTO-inlinable thunk call as any imported C++ function: no table, no tag, no check, no new row in §X.4.

edits.new:
There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are
  `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types. A C++
  header's several functions of one name reach Ember as one name (`[FFI-17g]`), not as `E1030`: the
  program declares none of them, and each use stands for one of them, chosen when compiling.
edits.why: [TYP-26] is where the refusal is caused; the exception states its reason (the functions are the header's, not the program's) and stays general over every kind of C++ name. §I.6's non-goal stands: an Ember program still cannot declare two functions of one name.

edits.old:
An overlay entry whose name, parameter count or parameter names
  do not match the header is `E5010`, so overlays cannot drift.
edits.new:
An overlay entry whose name, parameter count or parameter names
  do not match the header is `E5010`, so overlays cannot drift; so is an entry, a `rename` or a `hide`
  that fits none, or more than one, of a name's several functions (`[FFI-17g]`, `[GRM-35]`) by what it
  writes, the message naming each and the word to add ("`fn set(name: borrowed nul_terminated, value)`
  fits two functions of `Shader`, `set(const char*, int)` and `set(const char*, float)`; write the type
  that tells them apart: `value: c_int` or `value: f32`").
edits.why: An entry vouches for one function (verdict 131's problem was a line vouching for two). The refusal is at the rule that already matches entries, with the same code, and its message gives the line to write.

edits.new:
A function of a name that has several (`[FFI-17g]`) has a line of its own, keyed by the words of its
  entry that name it, quoted as TOML asks (`"Renderer.draw(mesh: Mesh)" = "blake3:…"`), its fingerprint
  that one declaration's, so that a changed parameter type of either function is a changed
  declaration; a default argument's expression is still not.
edits.why: The record keyed by name alone could hold one fingerprint for two functions; keyed by the entry's own words it checks each function the overlay describes (verdict 121: Ember writes the record, never a person), and the earlier design's "the key is tooling" hole closes.

edits.new:
For a name of several functions (`[FFI-17g]`) it writes one entry per function, with the
  parameters' words and types that tell them apart and no more.
edits.why: `ember bind --init` is where the starter overlay is written; a name of several functions needs one entry each, written with the least that names it.

edits.rule: FFI-48 table row "overloads differing only in return type"
edits.old: | overloads differing only in return type | Ember has no return-type overloading | rename one in the overlay |
edits.why: A C++ header cannot declare two functions differing only in the result (ill-formed), so the row refused nothing and sent the reader to a `rename` that could not name one overload. The case that can occur, two functions alike in all Ember sees (template instances differing only in the result; `int` and `long` where a target makes both `i32`), is refused at the call by `[FFI-17g]` (`E5035`) with a `hide` or `rename` by parameters as the way out, and the header stays imported.

edits.old: | `E5010` | overlay does not match the C declaration; a declaration an overlay describes differs from the one `ember.overlays` records, or the package has no record of the overlay; an entry outside a class section that names only members of classes | `[FFI-12]`, `[FFI-55]` |
edits.new: | `E5010` | overlay does not match the C declaration; a declaration an overlay describes differs from the one `ember.overlays` records, or the package has no record of the overlay; an entry outside a class section that names only members of classes; an entry, `rename` or `hide` that fits none or several of a name's C++ functions | `[FFI-12]`, `[FFI-55]` |
edits.why: The registry row names every case its defining rules give.

edits.rule: code table, new row after E5034
edits.old: | `E5034` | unsupported C++ construct | `[FFI-48]` |
edits.new:
| `E5034` | unsupported C++ construct | `[FFI-48]` |
| `E5035` | a use of a C++ name of several functions that none fits, or that several fit equally (a function declared `= delete` chosen included); a function value of such a name with no expected type | `[FFI-17g]` |
edits.why: One code, one defining rule: `E2070` stays [TYP-24]'s ambiguous interface method; the imported set gets its own code, defined by the new rule.

edits.old:
overlay_item  := {attribute} (overlay_fn | "type" IDENT NEWLINE | "enum" IDENT NEWLINE
                   | "rename" IDENT "as" IDENT NEWLINE | "hide" IDENT NEWLINE | extend_decl
                   | overlay_class)
  overlay_class := "class" IDENT ":" NEWLINE INDENT {{attribute} overlay_fn} DEDENT
  overlay_fn    := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT "(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")"
                   ["->" contract {contract}] NEWLINE
  overlay_param := IDENT [":" contract {contract}]
edits.new:
overlay_item  := {attribute} (overlay_fn | "type" IDENT NEWLINE | "enum" IDENT NEWLINE
                   | overlay_name | extend_decl | overlay_class)
  overlay_name  := "rename" member_ref "as" IDENT NEWLINE | "hide" member_ref NEWLINE
  overlay_class := "class" IDENT ":" NEWLINE INDENT {{attribute} (overlay_fn | overlay_name)} DEDENT
  overlay_fn    := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT "(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")"
                   ["->" (type {contract} | contract {contract})] NEWLINE
  overlay_param := [param_word] IDENT [":" [type] {contract}]
  member_ref    := IDENT ["(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")" ["->" type]]
edits.why: The one entry form gains the words Ember's own `param` already has (`[param_word] IDENT ":" type`), optional, and `rename`/`hide` gain a parameter list, so one line can name one of several functions and a member line can be renamed or hidden under its class (verdict 131). No second entry form, no C++ text in a string.

edits.new:
A parameter's word (`ref mut`, `owns`) and type, and the result's type, are written where they tell a
  name's several functions apart (`[FFI-17g]`), and may be written anywhere; each is the one the import
  gives (`[FFI-8]`, `[FFI-17a]`, `[FFI-40]`) and is checked against it (`[FFI-12]`). After the colon a
  word that is one of `[FFI-11]`'s is a contract word and any other is the type, so a type whose name is
  a contract word is first given another (`rename status as Status`); where one target's types make two
  functions alike, the importer's spelling tells them apart (`c_long` against `c_int`). An entry, a
  `rename` or a `hide` names one function: by the name alone where it has one, else by its parameters'
  count, names, words and types; `@ffi(const)` on a method's entry names the `const` one of two methods
  alike otherwise (`[FFI-40a]`, verdict 132). `rename` with parameters gives that function a name of its
  own, outside the set; `hide` with parameters removes it from the set; either needs no `unsafe`.
edits.why: States how the new grammar is read, with no new vocabulary: types are Ember's, contract words are the closed list of [FFI-11], and the one collision is solved by a `rename` the grammar already has.

edits.new:
* `[FFI-17g]` *(new in 0.9.20)* **Several C++ functions of one name.** A C++ name the header declares
  for several functions — a namespace's or a class's functions, a class's constructors (`new`), its
  static functions, a virtual method and its overloads, the instances of a function template listed in
  `instantiate=[…]` (`[FFI-17b]`), a function with default arguments counting once for each number of
  arguments it accepts (never a count that leaves out a parameter another parameter's contract word
  names), a redeclared function counting once (`[FFI-30]`) — is one Ember name, as `[FFI-40]`,
  `[FFI-41]` and `[FFI-44]` give it, and not `E1030` (`[TYP-26]`): the program declares none of them.
  Each use of the name stands for one function, chosen when compiling from the use's own words and
  nothing around it: (1) the functions the call's number of arguments and the names it gives fit; one
  left is chosen, and the call is then checked against it as any call (an untyped literal taking the
  type that parameter expects, `[LEX-16]`, `[LEX-17]`); (2) of several, the one whose parameters are
  the arguments' own types, an untyped literal counting as its default type (`int`, `f64`), and whose
  object a method's receiver fits as its name is (a name that may change the object fits a method that
  may change it, a name that only reads fits one that only reads, `[FFI-40]`; `this` is a name that may
  change the object where any other line of its method changes it, else one that only reads, as what a
  method does to its object is read from its code, `[CLS-7]`, verdict 86); (3) else the one every
  argument reaches by a coercion of `[TYP-5]`, an untyped literal as a type of its own kind (an
  integer literal a whole-number type, a float literal a float type), a name that may change the
  object reaching a method that only reads it as a view (`[TYP-5]` rule 7); of a `const` and a
  non-`const` method alike in all else as imported, the one without `const` (C++'s choice for an
  object that may change; an entry with `@ffi(const)` makes them differ, `[FFI-40a]`). A function
  declared `= delete` takes part and, chosen, is refused as deleted. None, or several at one step, is
  `E5035`, naming each function as the header declares it and why it does or does not fit, with the
  line to write ("`out.put(5)` (line 6) fits `void put(int v)` and `void put(long v)` of `io::Out`
  alike: `5` is a whole number either takes; write `out.put(5 as c_int)` or `out.put(5 as c_long)`;
  where this target makes `int` and `long` one type, hide the one not meant in the overlay, under
  `class Out:`: `hide put(v: c_long)`"). `super.init(…)` chooses the base constructor so
  (`[FFI-39b]`); an `override fn` matches one virtual method by its exact signature (`[FFI-39]`); a
  function value of the name is the function whose type its place expects exactly (`[TYP-5]` rule 10),
  and with no expected type `E5035`. What the code around the use permits — `unsafe:`, effects, the
  loop and view rules, what a name allows — is checked afterwards, on the chosen function, so a line
  stands for the same function wherever it stands. Each function has its own thunk (`[FFI-17]`), its
  own overlay entry (`[GRM-35]`, `[FFI-12]`), its own `@safety` and `L3015` (`[UNS-7]`, verdict 125)
  and its own line of `ember.overlays` (`[FFI-55]`); the chosen function is called as any imported C++
  function is, one direct call of its thunk, and nothing runs while the program runs for this rule.
edits.why: The missing rule, placed with the C++ import rules it governs. It is a property (a name of several functions and what a use's words fit), never a program's shape; it reuses the ranking Ember already has for one name's interface instances ([TYP-24], ODR-096) and the receiver rule [FFI-40] already states; it reads only the import and the use's own words, so a package decides it alone ([BLD-16]); and it adds no instruction to any call.

designs.runtime_cost: Nothing. Which function a use stands for is decided when compiling from the import and the use's own words; the chosen function is called as every imported C++ function already is: §X.4 row "FFI call | guaranteed present | one direct call for an ABI-direct C function", the thunk inlined under the project's LTO ([BLD-FFI-4]). No overload table, no type tag, no run-time test, no extra argument. A default argument costs exactly the C++ call site's cost: the arity's thunk passes what was given and the C++ compiler evaluates the default inside the thunk, as it would at a C++ call. The only new code is more thunks (one per function and per accepted arity), which is code size: implementation-defined under [COST-2], not a cost of running. [COST-5] asks for no new row because no instruction is added to any line.
designs.implementer_steps: 1. Importer (libclang, writing the `.embind` of [FFI-14]): within each namespace and class, group declarations by their Ember name ([FFI-40], [FFI-41], constructors under `new`), one function per Clang USR so redeclarations merge ([FFI-30]); for each function record its parameters (names, Ember type by the [FFI-8]/[FFI-17a]/[FFI-40] tables and the importer's spelling such as `c_long`, the word `ref mut`/`owns`), the method's `const` qualifier and what [FFI-40a] derives, `= delete`, the least count of arguments its default arguments allow, and the instances of each function template from `instantiate=[…]` ([FFI-17b]) as members of the template's name. 2. Thunk generation (`ember bind --emit-cpp`, [FFI-50]): for each function and each accepted arity emit one `extern "C"` thunk whose symbol is derived from the USR hash and the arity (so two packages importing one header emit the same symbol, given vague linkage or kept per package), calling the C++ function with the arguments given; the C++ compiler fills the defaults. 3. Name resolution in the type checker: an imported name resolves to its set; a call runs the three steps of [FFI-17g] before the ordinary call check, with step 2 and 3 reusing the fit tests the TYP-24/ODR-096 instance chooser already has (exact type; literal default type; the coercion list of [TYP-5]; a literal of its own kind); a function-value use consults the expected callable type only; `super.init` and `override fn` call the same matcher, the override in exact mode (E5056). 4. The receiver's kind comes from the place's declaration (local or `ref mut`: may change; plain parameter, loop or pattern name: reads); for `this`, compute the method's change summary with its calls to const/non-const pairs left out, then resolve those calls by the result (the fixed point verdict 86's inference already computes for every method); apply the `const` tie-break where the pair is alike. 5. Everything after selection is unchanged: E3023, E3100, L3015, the effect and loop rules run on the one chosen function. 6. Overlay matcher ([FFI-12], [GRM-35]): parse `[param_word] IDENT [":" [type] {contract}]`, classifying the first word after the colon by the closed [FFI-11] list; an entry, `rename` or `hide` maps to the functions it fits by name, count, names, words, types (by imported spelling), `@ffi(const)` and result type; zero or several is E5010 with the distinguishing word in the message; `rename` with parameters moves that function out of the set under the new name, `hide` drops it. 7. `ember.overlays` writer ([FFI-55]): one line per function keyed by the entry's own naming words, quoted for TOML; the fingerprint is already the canonical type plus names, so a changed overload is caught. 8. `ember bind --init` ([CLI-5]) writes one entry per function with the fewest words that name it; `--report` ([CLI-6]) may list each name whose functions this target's types make alike. 9. Diagnostics: an E5035 builder that prints each candidate as the header declares it, the step at which it fell out and why, and the cast or `hide` line; L3015 and E5010 name the function with the words that tell it apart. 10. Tests: the two programs above on gcc, clang and MSVC (the alias case differs by target); break tests per step (remove step 2 and `r.draw(mesh)` ties; remove the exact override rule and the KeyEvent override is accepted; remove the `const` tie-break and the out-of-line pair ties); `ember bind --emit-cpp` inspected for one thunk per function and arity; a run printing which overload ran.
designs.departs_from_verdict: none. Verdict 125 (a C++ function a program calls in unsafe code carries `@safety` in its entry) holds per function: each overload has its own entry and its own L3015. Verdict 131 (member lines under their class) holds, and `rename`/`hide` of a member go under the class too. Verdict 132 (`@ffi(const)` keeps a method const, an entry without it makes it changing) holds and is what names the `const` one of an alike pair. Verdict 121 (`ember.overlays` written by Ember, never by hand) holds; only its key becomes per function. Verdict 86 (what a method does to its object is read from its code) is what decides `this`. Verdict 117 and [TYP-26]'s pack clause are untouched.
designs.trade_offs: Speed: identical in every option considered (one name, mangled names, overlay-only names): a direct thunk call chosen when compiling; this design adds thunks per arity (code size) and one fit test per candidate per use at compile time, nothing else. Safety: refuses rather than guesses at every tie, matches overrides exactly (closing the earlier design's backwards-coercion hole), and checks `unsafe:`/E3023/effects on the one chosen function so a line never changes meaning by moving. Given up against C++: (a) no per-argument ranking and no promotion-before-conversion, so a narrow number or a bare literal among `int`/`long`/`long long`/`double` overloads that C++ ranks is refused with a cast as the way out (`lives as c_int`, `5 as c_int`); (b) a bare literal is Ember's `int` (i64), so between `f(int)` and `f(long long)` it is exact on the latter where C++ takes the former, kept because one literal has one meaning everywhere ([TYP-24], [LEX-16]) rather than a C++ meaning inside C++ calls; (c) Ember may pick one function where C++ is ambiguous (an `i64` literal for `value(int64_t)`/`value(double)`), never one C++ would not consider. Readability: ordinary C++ lines compile unchanged; overlay entries carry a word or type only where parameter names do not tell functions apart; `this` resolves by the method's inferred constness, which is not written on the line, as no change fact is since verdict 86. Consistency: one rule for calls, `super.init`, overrides, function values and overlay entries; no second entry form; `rename`/`hide` gain the parameter list that FFI-48's "rename one in the overlay" always needed.
designs.remaining_doubt: (1) `c_int` and `c_long` are aliases (§XV: "`c_int` and the other C aliases"), so on MSVC `f(int)`/`f(long)` are alike to Ember and every call ties until an overlay `hide`; a program portable across targets writes that line, or `c_long` becomes a distinct type, which is another question (E1-12). (2) Instances of one function template that differ only in template arguments or the result tie; the overlay names one by `rename get() -> f64 as get_f64`, but an Ember spelling of an instance at the call (`eng.get[f64]()`) belongs to the templates question ([FFI-17b]). (3) `this` deciding by the method's other lines is the owner's style (verdict 86) but not his ruling; the alternative, `this` always a name that may change, costs nothing more and refuses the wrapper-class pattern through plain parameters. (4) A C++ parameter the header leaves unnamed cannot be given by name at a call or told apart by name in an entry; the type then does the work. (5) The const/non-const `operator[]` pair goes through `Index`/`IndexMut` ([FFI-42]), not this selection: K47's question, unchanged here. (6) The exact wording of E5035 and of the per-overload L3015 is the lead's.

designs.question: K21: How do C++ overloaded functions and constructors import into Ember? (How an overload set is named, how a use picks one member, how ambiguity is refused, how an overlay entry names one overload, what `ember bind` writes, the codes; default arguments and const/non-const pairs included.)
designs.summary: A C++ name the header declares several times imports as one Ember name of several members, one per declaration (a const/non-const pair is first split into `at` and `at_mut`, as `get`/`get_mut` and `span`/`span_mut` already are; a default argument gives one member per arity, its thunk letting C++ supply the default). Each use stands for the one member its own words fit — the arguments' number, the word before each (`ref mut`, `owns`, none) and their types, an exact fit before a coercion as `[TYP-24]` already ranks, an untyped literal exact for C++'s `int`/`double` — and only then is the chosen member checked for `unsafe:`, read-only names and effects, so the same line runs the same function wherever it stands; none or a tie is `E5035` naming each member's first line and the cast or `rename` line to write. An overlay entry, `rename` or `hide` of such a name writes each parameter's type (`fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`), so it names exactly one declaration and `ember.overlays` keys it per member; an `override fn` matches a virtual member exactly, an upcast or widening counting for nothing (`E5056`). Nothing runs while the program runs: a use is a direct call of the member's own thunk, named by its mangled name.

edits.new: * `[FFI-57]` *(new in 0.9.20)* **A name declared several times.** A C++ name the header declares with several parameter lists — a function of a namespace, a method, a static member function, a constructor (`new`, `[GRM-35]`), or the explicit instantiations of one template (`[FFI-17b]`) — imports as one Ember name of several **members**, one per declaration, each with its own thunk (`[FFI-17]`), its own identity (`[FFI-30]`), its own entry and its own line of `ember.overlays` (`[FFI-55]`). A const and a non-const pair is split first (`[FFI-40b]`), and a parameter with a default argument makes its function a name of several members too: one per arity the defaults allow, each arity's thunk calling the function with the trailing arguments left out, so that C++ supplies the defaults as it would at a call of its own. Each use of such a name stands for one member, read from the use alone. A call (a method call, `T.new(…)`, `super.init(…)`, `[FFI-39b]`) fits a member when that member, declared alone, would accept its arguments: their number, the word before each (`ref mut`, `owns`, none: `[FN-2a]`, `[FFI-40]`) and their types under `[TYP-5]`; of the members it fits, one whose every parameter's type is its argument's own type — an untyped literal counting as its own for a parameter whose C++ type is `int` (a whole number) or `double` (a fraction), the types C++ gives those literals — is chosen before one that some argument reaches only through a coercion (`[TYP-24]`). A name used without a call stands for the member whose first line is exactly the callable type expected there (`[CLO-3]`). What the code around the use allows — unsafe code (`[FFI-2]`), a read-only name (`E3023`), its effects — is checked after, on the member chosen, so one line stands for one member wherever it is written. A use that fits no member, or two with none exact, is `E5035`, which names each member by its first line and why it does not fit and, for a tie, the argument to write with its type or the `rename` line that gives one member a name of its own: "`c.show(lives)` fits two members of `ui.Counter.show`, `show(value: c_int)` and `show(value: i64)`, each by widening `lives` (`u8`); write `lives as c_int` or `lives as i64`". Two members whose first lines are one on the target compiled for (`put(v: c_int)` and `put(v: c_long)` where `long` is 32 bits) fit every call together; the `rename` line tells them apart on every target, since an overlay writes the table's spelling of the C++ type (`c_long` for `long`, `[FFI-8]`, `[FFI-17a]`), not the target's width. The entry of a member in an overlay writes each parameter's type, as the import maps the C++ type, as the first word after its colon, before its contract words (`fn set(name: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated, value: f32)`), and so does a `rename` or `hide` of one member (`rename put(v: c_long) as put_long`, `[GRM-35]`); an entry, `rename` or `hide` of such a name that writes no type, or whose types name no member or two, is `E5010`, whose message gives each member's entry line (`[FFI-12]`); an entry of a name declared once is written as before. `L3015` (`[UNS-7]`) and `E5002` (`[FFI-2]`) give a member's typed entry line. `ember bind --report` lists each name of several members with the first line of each; `ember bind --emit-cpp` writes one thunk per member, named by the member's mangled name (`[MNG-1]`). Nothing runs for this while the program runs: a use is one direct call of the member's thunk, as any imported C++ function's.
edits.why: Annex C is silent on the construct nearly every C++ header has. The rule is a property (a name declared several times), decided from the header and the line alone (`[BLD-16]`), with no coercion ranking beyond `[TYP-24]`'s, so a call never silently runs a member C++ would not and is refused, with the line to write, wherever it is unclear.

edits.new: * `[FFI-40b]` *(new in 0.9.20)* **A const and a non-const pair.** A non-`const` method beside a `const` method of the same name and the same parameters, as the import maps them, imports with `_mut` added to its name — `at` and `at_mut`, as `get` and `get_mut` (`[FFI-42]`) and `span` and `span_mut` (`[FFI-17a]`) — so the two are two names, and which one a call runs is read from the call (`cfg.at(i)`, `cfg.at_mut(i).port = 8080`), never from the name the object is reached through nor from the lines after it; `at_mut` may change its object (`[FFI-40]`), and the `const` one is read as `[FFI-40a]` says. An overlay entry names each by its Ember name (`@ffi(const) fn at(i)`, `fn at_mut(i)`, `[FFI-12]`). A class that itself declares `at_mut` beside such a pair is the `[FFI-48]` row.
edits.why: Choosing by the receiver's kind is circular inside a class method (whether `this` may change is worked out from the body that contains the call) and lets a read-only parameter silently run another function than a local does. Two names make the choice a word on the line, which Ember's bridge already does for `get_mut` and `span_mut`, and let an overlay vouch for either member.

edits.old: There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types.
edits.new: There is no overloading: two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`, except operator-interface implementations and `extend` blocks for different types. A C++ name a header declares several times is one Ember name of several members, each use standing for one (`[FFI-57]`): the declarations are the header's, which a program cannot change, and a function Ember declares beside an imported name is `E1030` as any other.
edits.why: The rule as written refuses every C++ class with two constructors; the exception says where it stops and why.

edits.old: implicit numeric narrowing; function overloading
edits.new: implicit numeric narrowing; function overloading (a C++ header's overloads import as one name of several members, each use standing for one, `[FFI-57]`)
edits.why: The non-goal stays true for Ember's own functions; the cross-reference stops a reader finding Annex C contradicting Part I.

edits.old: one thunk per imported function, method, constructor and destructor
edits.new: one thunk per imported function, method, constructor and destructor, a name declared several times giving one per member and a default argument one per arity (`[FFI-57]`)
edits.why: The thunk count is where a reader of this rule asks what two constructors become.

edits.old: `super.init(…)` selects the C++ base constructor by arity and argument types and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`); a base with no default constructor and no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.new: `super.init(…)` runs the C++ base constructor its arguments select as `[FFI-57]` selects a member of the base's `new` (an exact fit before a coercion; none or a tie `E5035`) and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`); a base with no default constructor and no declared `init` is `E5058`.
edits.why: One selection rule for constructors wherever they are called; "by arity and argument types" said neither how a literal counts nor what a tie is.

edits.old: An `override fn` matching no virtual method of the base, by name and signature, is `E5056`.
edits.new: An `override fn` matching no virtual method of the base, by name and first line — each parameter's word and type exactly those the import gives the virtual method's (`[FFI-40]`), and its result; an upcast or a widening counts for nothing, since C++ hands the override its own argument (a `FocusEvent` for an `on(const Event&)`) — is `E5056`, whose message gives each virtual method of that name as the `override fn` line to write; where the base declares the name several times (`[FFI-57]`), the override replaces the one member it matches and the trampoline passes on that one, the others staying the base's.
edits.why: An override matched through an upcast would read a smaller base object as a derived one in safe code, and one matched through a widening would truncate C++'s argument: both are what the checker exists to refuse. "By name and signature" is made exact and told how an overloaded virtual is replaced.

edits.old: An overlay entry whose name, parameter count or parameter names do not match the header is `E5010`, so overlays cannot drift.
edits.new: An overlay entry whose name (a member's Ember name, `at_mut` for `[FFI-40b]`'s), parameter count or parameter names do not match the header, or, for a name declared several times, whose parameter types name no member or two (`[FFI-57]`), is `E5010`, so overlays cannot drift and no entry vouches for a function it does not name.
edits.why: Name, count and parameter names cannot tell `set(const char*, int)` from `set(const char*, float)`; an entry must name one declaration or it vouches for one nobody looked at.

edits.new: A member of a name declared several times (`[FFI-57]`) has a line of its own, keyed by the declaration as the header spells it, quoted (`"gfx::Renderer::draw(const gfx::Mesh&)" = "blake3:…"`); a `rename` in the overlay changes its key not at all.
edits.why: The record is keyed by name; with two declarations of one name the check of verdict 121 would compare an entry against the wrong declaration or lose one.

edits.old: a later file's `override` entry replaces an earlier file's for that name, and any other second entry for one name is `E5010` (ODR-149).
edits.new: a later file's `override` entry replaces an earlier file's for that name — for a name declared several times, for the member its types name (`[FFI-57]`) — and any other second entry for one name or member is `E5010` (ODR-149).
edits.why: Composition counts entries by name; two typed entries for two members of one name are not a second entry for one name.
